# Computing Before Equilibrium: Cold-Start Compensation for Microring Photonic Accelerators

## Summary

Photonic matrix processors are usually evaluated after their lasers, heaters, and resonators have reached thermal equilibrium. That assumption is poorly matched to intermittently powered systems, such as battery-limited sensor nodes and accelerators that are power-gated between bursts. A microring array may perform a multiplication in nanoseconds yet spend substantially longer warming, calibrating, and locking its weights. The resulting delay and energy are absent from most throughput figures.

This project proposes **Kestrel**, a cold-start compensation method that permits useful matrix multiplication during thermal settling. Rather than forcing every resonator immediately to its equilibrium state, Kestrel will infer the array’s evolving optical operator from a small set of pilot wavelengths. It will then apply a low-rank electronic correction to each optical output. The central premise is that startup drift is high-dimensional at the device level but low-dimensional at the matrix level because many rings share heaters, substrate paths, and ambient conditions.

The project will test whether this structure can reduce time-to-first-valid-result and total energy per valid multiply without requiring continuous per-ring locking.

## Research questions and hypotheses

The primary question is: **Can a resonator-based photonic matrix engine compute accurately before thermal equilibrium, once startup drift is represented as a low-dimensional operator?**

Three hypotheses will be tested:

1. Across repeated power cycles, at least 95% of the variance in the array-level weight error can be represented by six or fewer calibrated drift modes.
2. Four pilot wavelengths, observed at eight monitor ports, can estimate the coefficients of those modes well enough to keep normalized matrix error below 2% during most of the startup interval.
3. Including pilot generation, monitor detection, conversion, and digital correction, Kestrel will reduce energy to the first 1,000 valid matrix-vector products by at least 40% relative to waiting for equilibrium.

These hypotheses separate physical structure, observability, and system benefit. A low-rank drift model alone would not establish an advantage if estimating or correcting it consumed excessive energy.

## Proposed architecture

Let the programmed equilibrium operator be $W_0$. During startup, the realized operator is modeled as

$$W(t) = W_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{K} z_k(t) B_k + R(t),$$

where the matrices $B_k$ are drift modes learned during calibration, $z_k(t)$ are time-varying coefficients, and $R(t)$ is unmodeled residual error. Each $B_k$ will be factorized as $P_kQ_k^T$ with rank at most two. After the photonic core produces $y_p=W(t)x$, a small electronic unit will calculate

$$y_c = y_p - \sum_k z_k(t)P_k(Q_k^Tx).$$

This correction scales with the number and rank of drift modes rather than with the full matrix size. Pilot tones placed between data channels will traverse the same distribution network as the computational wavelengths. Their monitor-port intensities will be mapped to $z_k(t)$ by a ridge-regression estimator initially, followed by a compact nonlinear estimator only if residual analysis shows a clear need.

Kestrel differs from conventional locking in its objective. It does not attempt to return every ring to its nominal resonance at every instant. It estimates the aggregate computational error and corrects only the components that materially affect the output.

## Experimental plan

### Phase 1: Drift characterization

A 64-by-64 wavelength-multiplexed microring test array will be instrumented with heater telemetry, eight optical monitor ports, and synchronized output capture. Two dies from the same fabrication run will be tested. Each die will undergo 1,000 startup cycles at ambient set points of 15, 25, and 40 degrees Celsius, with three input-power levels and randomized idle durations.

During each cycle, 256 probe vectors will be repeated from laser turn-on until equilibrium. The instantaneous matrix will be reconstructed from the outputs, and principal-component and structured low-rank analyses will identify recurring drift modes. Calibration and evaluation cycles will be separated by day to prevent the model from merely interpolating adjacent traces.

The principal endpoint is the fraction of matrix-error variance captured as a function of mode count. Secondary analyses will determine whether mode shapes transfer between temperatures, power levels, and dies.

### Phase 2: Pilot-based state estimation

Candidate pilot sets will be selected by maximizing sensitivity to the calibrated drift modes while minimizing spectral interference with data channels. Estimators will be trained on 60% of startup cycles, tuned on 20%, and evaluated on the remaining 20%, with complete cycles—not individual timestamps—assigned to each split.

Ablations will vary the number of pilots, monitor ports, modes, and temporal history samples. To distinguish genuine state observation from a learned startup clock, one control will provide only elapsed time since power-on. Further controls will perturb ambient temperature midway through startup and introduce randomized laser ramp profiles. Success requires the pilot estimator to outperform the clock-only model under both perturbations.

### Phase 3: End-to-end computing tests

Kestrel will be evaluated on three workload classes: dense random matrices spanning several condition numbers, convolutional layers extracted from a compact acoustic event classifier, and a recurrent layer used for vibration-anomaly detection. For each workload, results will be labeled valid when they meet a task-specific output-error threshold established using equilibrium operation.

Comparators will include: waiting for passive equilibrium; static one-time trimming; heater feedback using all available monitors; and a time-indexed correction without pilots. Measurements will report time-to-first-valid-result, valid results per joule over burst lengths from 10 to 100,000 operations, normalized matrix error, task accuracy, and the 99th-percentile error across startups.

Energy accounting will include lasers, thermal tuning, pilot generation, photodiodes, data converters, and the correction unit. Both measured board-level power and a component-normalized projection will be reported so that an inefficient laboratory controller is not mistaken for an architectural cost.

## Decision criteria and failure analysis

Kestrel will be considered successful if it achieves less than 2% median normalized matrix error from 50 microseconds after turn-on until equilibrium, limits 99th-percentile error to 5%, and reduces energy to the first 1,000 valid operations by at least 40% on both dies. Results that meet accuracy targets but lose the energy advantage after accounting for conversion and correction will be treated as a negative system result.

If drift is not low-rank, spatially partitioned models will be tested by assigning separate modes to quadrants of the array. If pilot observability is inadequate, pilots will be moved from shared monitor ports to sparse taps within the mesh. These alternatives increase hardware overhead and will therefore be evaluated against the same energy criteria rather than accepted solely for improving accuracy.

## Expected contribution

The project will produce a cycle-resolved dataset of photonic startup behavior, a method for determining whether thermal transients are computationally compressible, and an experimentally grounded comparison between settling, locking, and error correction. More broadly, it reframes startup as an operating regime rather than dead time. If successful, Kestrel would make photonic acceleration more credible for bursty workloads, where equilibrium throughput is a poor predictor of delivered efficiency.

# The Clock Between Plays: Restart Latency as a Tactical Signal in Team Sports

## Scope of the literature

Restart latency—the time between an official stoppage and the next live phase—has received less attention than possession, shot quality, or player movement. Yet restarts occupy a substantial portion of many matches and may reveal tactical intent. A team that restarts quickly might be trying to exploit a disorganised defence, while a slower team might be conserving energy or protecting a lead. This review considers whether restart latency can function as a performance indicator across football, futsal, handball, and field hockey.

The review covers work published from 2016 to 2025. Searches used the terms “restart speed,” “dead-ball duration,” “stoppage tempo,” and “time to resume” in the ScholarSport and FieldIndex databases. Eleven quantitative studies and two conference papers were retained because they reported either restart time or a similar measure. Studies focused only on broadcast scheduling were excluded. The search suggests that restart analysis is a small but rapidly developing area, although related work using terms such as “ball recovery interval” may have been missed.

## Definitions and measurement

The literature does not use a single definition. Neral and Voss (2017) measured football throw-in latency from the moment the ball crossed the touchline until it re-entered play. The Kestrel Match Lab (2019) started its clock when the referee signalled direction, producing shorter values. In handball, Pellin et al. (2021) included the time needed for substitutions after goals, whereas Yarrow and Tem (2023) excluded substitution time as an administrative delay. These differences matter because two studies can report different average latencies without observing different behaviour.

Most researchers use event logs or manually coded video. Event logs permit analysis of thousands of restarts but often record only whole seconds. Manual coding is more precise but introduces judgement about when a stoppage begins. Only Baret and Quil (2022) reported a reliability test: two coders agreed within 0.4 seconds for 86% of 240 hockey restarts. This seems sufficient for broad tactical categories, such as fast, normal, and slow, but perhaps not for claims involving differences of less than one second. Median latency appears preferable to mean latency because a small number of injuries or equipment delays can distort a match average.

## Tactical findings

The most consistent finding is that restart latency changes with score. Neral and Voss found that teams leading after the 70th minute took 3.1 seconds longer over throw-ins than teams that were level. A similar pattern appeared in the North Coast Futsal Dataset, where trailing teams resumed after goals more quickly (Kestrel Match Lab, 2019). Because the same relationship occurs in two sports, it probably represents a general strategic response rather than a rule-specific feature. However, both studies treated each restart as independent even though restarts were clustered within matches and teams.

Several papers connect fast restarts with attacking success. In 62 field hockey matches, Baret and Quil reported that circle entries were more common within 20 seconds of a restart when the restart itself took under five seconds. Aven Torrel (2020) found that quick football free kicks generated 0.08 expected goals per sequence, compared with 0.05 after slower free kicks. This indicates that restarting quickly improves attack quality, probably because opponents have less time to organise. The comparison is not entirely secure, since teams may choose quick restarts only when an attractive attacking option already exists. Torrel controlled for pitch zone but not defensive numbers or the identity of the team.

The evidence for defensive effects is weaker. Yarrow and Tem observed fewer successful handball attacks after delays exceeding eight seconds and argued that slow restarts allow defensive substitutions. Pellin et al., using the same sport, found almost no relationship once score margin was included. The difference may result from competition level: Yarrow and Tem studied an elite league, while Pellin et al. combined university and regional matches. Overall, slow restarts seem to benefit defences, but the size of the benefit cannot be established because the studies report different outcomes.

## Fatigue, officials, and crowd effects

Restart latency has also been proposed as an indirect fatigue measure. The Brindle Arena Project (2024) found that median latency increased by 1.7 seconds from the first to the final quarter of futsal matches. The authors linked this change to physical fatigue, but late-game score management offers another explanation. No study reviewed here combined restart timing with physiological measures. Consequently, restart latency should not yet be treated as a substitute for tracking-based workload measures, though it could be useful when tracking data are unavailable.

Officials and venue conditions further complicate interpretation. Seln, Miro, and Dast (2022) reported longer hockey restarts under officials who issued more verbal instructions. In contrast, the Vale Indoor Study (2023) attributed most variation to crowd noise, because players took longer to recognise signals in louder venues. Crowd noise and official behaviour were not included in the same model, so either factor may be standing in for the other. Nonetheless, both studies show that restart time is not purely a team-controlled decision.

## Analytical value and future use

The literature supports three possible uses of restart latency: describing game management, identifying fast-attack opportunities, and detecting unusual delays. The first is currently the strongest. Analysts could split latency by restart type, score state, and match period to create a simple tactical profile. A single match-level average would conceal whether a team is consistently slow or merely experienced one lengthy interruption.

More complicated models may not be necessary. A threshold of five seconds separates fast and slow restarts in several papers and is easy for coaches to interpret. The same threshold could be applied across sports, allowing clubs to compare restart discipline between squads. Rule differences are a limitation, but all four sports reward teams that act before opponents are organised. Future studies should test whether reducing latency through training causes more successful attacks, ideally by comparing matches before and after a restart routine is introduced.

## Conclusion

Restart latency is a measurable and tactically meaningful feature that conventional performance summaries overlook. Existing studies broadly associate quicker restarts with trailing score states and improved attacking outcomes, while slower restarts are linked to lead protection, defensive organisation, and possibly fatigue. The evidence remains fragmented because definitions vary and contextual variables are handled inconsistently. Even so, the recurrence of similar patterns across several sports suggests that restart latency deserves inclusion in routine team analysis, especially where detailed player-tracking data are unavailable.

- Brindle Arena Project. (2024). *Temporal drift in indoor match stoppages*. Brindle Performance Papers.
- Kestrel Match Lab. (2019). *Goal restarts and score state in North Coast futsal*. Technical Report 14.
- Neral, P., & Voss, E. (2017). Touchline delay as strategic behaviour. *Football Event Review, 3*(1), 18–32.

# Pause Before Consensus: Testing Batch-Released Deliberation in Journal Peer Review

## Summary

Peer-review reform usually focuses on who reviewers are, whether their names are disclosed, or how editors select them. This project instead examines the timing of reviewer interaction. In many editorial systems, the first reviewer to enter a discussion can frame the manuscript’s central problem before other reviewers have stated their positions. Later comments may then converge on that framing, even when initial reports emphasized different issues.

The proposed study will test a “batch-release” discussion protocol. Reviewers will submit short opening positions that remain sealed until every participating reviewer has responded or a 36-hour window expires. The statements will then be displayed simultaneously in randomized order. This protocol will be compared with an otherwise similar discussion in which each opening statement appears as soon as it is submitted. The study asks whether removing a temporally privileged first voice preserves independent information, changes editorial decisions, and improves agreement with a later assessment panel.

## Rationale

Reviewer disagreement is commonly treated as a problem to be resolved. Yet some disagreement reflects complementary expertise rather than error. A methods reviewer may identify an estimation problem while a domain reviewer notices that the research question is unimportant. If the first discussion comment defines one concern as decisive, other concerns may receive less attention without being answered.

Research on group judgment suggests that early statements can anchor later discussion, but journal peer review is an unusual setting: participants have already produced independent reports, possess unequal expertise, and know that an editor rather than the group makes the final decision. Findings from ordinary committees therefore may not transfer directly. A change to discussion timing is also comparatively inexpensive. It does not require publishing reviewer identities, recruiting additional reviewers, or changing a journal’s acceptance threshold.

## Research questions and hypotheses

The study will address three questions:

1. Does batch release reduce the influence of the earliest commenter on reviewers’ final recommendations?
2. Does it preserve a wider range of substantively distinct concerns without reducing useful consensus?
3. Do decisions reached under batch release correspond more closely to an independent panel’s later assessment?

The main hypothesis is that final recommendations in the conventional condition will be disproportionately associated with the earliest commenter’s pre-discussion score. Batch release is expected to weaken this association. It is also expected to increase the number of distinct concerns carried into the editor’s decision letter, while adding no more than one day to median decision time.

## Study design

The Meridian Editorial Cooperative, an invented consortium of twelve mid-volume journals in environmental engineering, computational linguistics, and behavioral economics, will participate for eighteen months. The target sample is 1,200 manuscripts that reach discussion with at least three completed reviews. Desk rejections, single-reviewer decisions, and manuscripts requiring an immediate ethics referral will be excluded.

Manuscripts will be randomized within journal and calendar month after all initial reports have been filed. In both conditions, reviewers will receive the same prompt asking for a 150-word opening position containing: a provisional recommendation on a five-point scale, the most decision-relevant concern, and one reason their recommendation might change.

In the sequential condition, each opening position will become visible to the other reviewers when submitted. In the batch-release condition, positions will remain sealed until all reviewers respond or 36 hours pass. Released statements will appear together in a computer-randomized order. Editors will be asked not to intervene before the opening stage closes. Afterward, both groups will use the journal’s ordinary unstructured discussion interface for up to five days. Editors will retain full authority over decisions.

Reviewers will be informed about the study when accepting the assignment and may decline participation without declining the review. Editors cannot be blinded because the interface will display the assigned protocol. Authors will not be told the condition until the study concludes, and the condition will not affect what information appears in decision letters.

## Measures

The primary behavioral outcome will be “first-position pull”: the extent to which reviewers’ final scores move toward the pre-discussion score of the earliest commenter in the sequential condition, compared with movement toward a randomly designated position in the batch-release condition. The model will adjust for every reviewer’s initial score, self-rated expertise, report length, and the initial distance between reviewers.

Secondary outcomes will include change in score dispersion, discussion length, time to decision, reviewer satisfaction, and the number of distinct concerns appearing both in discussion and in the editor’s letter. Two trained coders, unaware of condition, will classify concerns into design, analysis, interpretation, novelty, presentation, and ethics categories. Twenty percent of discussions will be double-coded, with disagreements resolved by a third coder. An exploratory text-similarity analysis will estimate whether later comments reuse the first commenter’s framing.

Decision quality will be estimated for a stratified random subset of 180 manuscripts. Six months after the original decision, a three-person assessment panel will receive the anonymized initial manuscript, revision if one exists, and editor letter, but not the original reviewer discussion or experimental condition. The panel will rate methodological soundness, contribution, and whether the original editorial decision was defensible. Distance between the editor’s decision and the panel median will serve as the principal quality measure. For accepted papers, eighteen-month citation counts and formal corrections will be recorded as exploratory outcomes.

## Analysis and sample size

The primary analysis will follow assignment regardless of whether all reviewers submit an opening position. A multilevel regression will include random intercepts for journal, editor, reviewer, and manuscript, since some reviewers and editors will appear repeatedly. Interaction terms will examine whether effects differ by initial disagreement, reviewer expertise, and field. The coding and analysis plan will be registered before outcomes are inspected.

With 1,200 manuscripts and an anticipated 15% rate of incomplete opening statements, the study is expected to have 80% power to detect a difference of approximately 0.14 standard deviations in first-position pull. This calculation treats manuscripts as independent and will be revised after the cooperative supplies estimates of repeat-reviewer frequency. No adjustment is planned for the exploratory subgroup comparisons.

## Practical and ethical considerations

Batch release may delay discussion when one reviewer does not respond. The 36-hour release rule limits this cost, and automatic reminders will be sent after 24 hours. A technical log will record accidental early disclosure, editor intervention, and interface failures. Manuscripts affected by such failures will remain in the main analysis but will also be examined separately.

The principal ethical concern is that authors are exposed to an unproven process. Both protocols preserve ordinary editorial authority, and editors may end discussion immediately if delay would harm an author. Reviewer comments and identifiers will be stored separately, and published results will aggregate journals unless a journal requests attribution.

## Limitations

The intervention combines two features—simultaneous release and randomized display order—so the study may not identify which feature causes any observed effect. The assessment panel is also another form of peer review rather than an objective measure of correctness. Because only twelve volunteer journals participate, results may not generalize to high-volume, highly selective, or non-English-language venues. Reviewers who consent to the experiment may be unusually comfortable with structured deliberation, and awareness of observation could make both conditions more careful than normal.

## Outputs

The project will produce a reusable discussion module, an anonymized dataset of score changes and coded concerns, and a protocol that journals can adapt without altering anonymity policies. If batch release reduces first-position pull without delaying decisions or lowering panel agreement, the cooperative will test it as the default discussion setting for a further year.

# Pause Before Consensus: Testing Batch-Released Deliberation in Journal Peer Review

## Summary

Peer-review reform usually focuses on who reviewers are, whether their names are disclosed, or how editors select them. This project instead examines the timing of reviewer interaction. In many editorial systems, the first reviewer to enter a discussion can frame the manuscript’s central problem before other reviewers have stated their positions. Later comments may then converge on that framing, even when initial reports emphasized different issues.

The proposed study will test a “batch-release” discussion protocol. Reviewers will submit short opening positions that remain sealed until every participating reviewer has responded or a 36-hour window expires. The statements will then be displayed simultaneously in randomized order. This protocol will be compared with an otherwise similar discussion in which each opening statement appears as soon as it is submitted. The study asks whether removing a temporally privileged first voice preserves independent information, changes editorial decisions, and improves agreement with a later assessment panel.

## Rationale

Reviewer disagreement is commonly treated as a problem to be resolved. Yet some disagreement reflects complementary expertise rather than error. A methods reviewer may identify an estimation problem while a domain reviewer notices that the research question is unimportant. If the first discussion comment defines one concern as decisive, other concerns may receive less attention without being answered.

Research on group judgment suggests that early statements can anchor later discussion, but journal peer review is an unusual setting: participants have already produced independent reports, possess unequal expertise, and know that an editor rather than the group makes the final decision. Findings from ordinary committees therefore may not transfer directly. A change to discussion timing is also comparatively inexpensive. It does not require publishing reviewer identities, recruiting additional reviewers, or changing a journal’s acceptance threshold.

## Research questions and hypotheses

The study will address three questions:

1. Does batch release reduce the influence of the earliest commenter on reviewers’ final recommendations?
2. Does it preserve a wider range of substantively distinct concerns without reducing useful consensus?
3. Do decisions reached under batch release correspond more closely to an independent panel’s later assessment?

The main hypothesis is that final recommendations in the conventional condition will be disproportionately associated with the earliest commenter’s pre-discussion score. Batch release is expected to weaken this association. It is also expected to increase the number of distinct concerns carried into the editor’s decision letter, while adding no more than one day to median decision time.

## Study design

The Meridian Editorial Cooperative, an invented consortium of twelve mid-volume journals in environmental engineering, computational linguistics, and behavioral economics, will participate for eighteen months. The target sample is 1,200 manuscripts that reach discussion with at least three completed reviews. Desk rejections, single-reviewer decisions, and manuscripts requiring an immediate ethics referral will be excluded.

Manuscripts will be randomized within journal and calendar month after all initial reports have been filed. In both conditions, reviewers will receive the same prompt asking for a 150-word opening position containing: a provisional recommendation on a five-point scale, the most decision-relevant concern, and one reason their recommendation might change.

In the sequential condition, each opening position will become visible to the other reviewers when submitted. In the batch-release condition, positions will remain sealed until all reviewers respond or 36 hours pass. Released statements will appear together in a computer-randomized order. Editors will be asked not to intervene before the opening stage closes. Afterward, both groups will use the journal’s ordinary unstructured discussion interface for up to five days. Editors will retain full authority over decisions.

Reviewers will be informed about the study when accepting the assignment and may decline participation without declining the review. Editors cannot be blinded because the interface will display the assigned protocol. Authors will not be told the condition until the study concludes, and the condition will not affect what information appears in decision letters.

## Measures

The primary behavioral outcome will be “first-position pull”: the extent to which reviewers’ final scores move toward the pre-discussion score of the earliest commenter in the sequential condition, compared with movement toward a randomly designated position in the batch-release condition. The model will adjust for every reviewer’s initial score, self-rated expertise, report length, and the initial distance between reviewers.

Secondary outcomes will include change in score dispersion, discussion length, time to decision, reviewer satisfaction, and the number of distinct concerns appearing both in discussion and in the editor’s letter. Two trained coders, unaware of condition, will classify concerns into design, analysis, interpretation, novelty, presentation, and ethics categories. Twenty percent of discussions will be double-coded, with disagreements resolved by a third coder. An exploratory text-similarity analysis will estimate whether later comments reuse the first commenter’s framing.

Decision quality will be estimated for a stratified random subset of 180 manuscripts. Six months after the original decision, a three-person assessment panel will receive the anonymized initial manuscript, revision if one exists, and editor letter, but not the original reviewer discussion or experimental condition. The panel will rate methodological soundness, contribution, and whether the original editorial decision was defensible. Distance between the editor’s decision and the panel median will serve as the principal quality measure. For accepted papers, eighteen-month citation counts and formal corrections will be recorded as exploratory outcomes.

## Analysis and sample size

The primary analysis will follow assignment regardless of whether all reviewers submit an opening position. A multilevel regression will include random intercepts for journal, editor, reviewer, and manuscript, since some reviewers and editors will appear repeatedly. Interaction terms will examine whether effects differ by initial disagreement, reviewer expertise, and field. The coding and analysis plan will be registered before outcomes are inspected.

With 1,200 manuscripts and an anticipated 15% rate of incomplete opening statements, the study is expected to have 80% power to detect a difference of approximately 0.14 standard deviations in first-position pull. This calculation treats manuscripts as independent and will be revised after the cooperative supplies estimates of repeat-reviewer frequency. No adjustment is planned for the exploratory subgroup comparisons.

## Practical and ethical considerations

Batch release may delay discussion when one reviewer does not respond. The 36-hour release rule limits this cost, and automatic reminders will be sent after 24 hours. A technical log will record accidental early disclosure, editor intervention, and interface failures. Manuscripts affected by such failures will remain in the main analysis but will also be examined separately.

The principal ethical concern is that authors are exposed to an unproven process. Both protocols preserve ordinary editorial authority, and editors may end discussion immediately if delay would harm an author. Reviewer comments and identifiers will be stored separately, and published results will aggregate journals unless a journal requests attribution.

## Limitations

The intervention combines two features—simultaneous release and randomized display order—so the study may not identify which feature causes any observed effect. The assessment panel is also another form of peer review rather than an objective measure of correctness. Because only twelve volunteer journals participate, results may not generalize to high-volume, highly selective, or non-English-language venues. Reviewers who consent to the experiment may be unusually comfortable with structured deliberation, and awareness of observation could make both conditions more careful than normal.

## Outputs

The project will produce a reusable discussion module, an anonymized dataset of score changes and coded concerns, and a protocol that journals can adapt without altering anonymity policies. If batch release reduces first-position pull without delaying decisions or lowering panel agreement, the cooperative will test it as the default discussion setting for a further year.

# Groundsong S4: Benthic-Contact Acoustic Monitoring System

## 1. Product summary

Groundsong S4 is a retrievable seabed array that detects and classifies events likely to disturb shallow-water habitats: anchor drops, dragging anchor or mooring chain, trawl-door passage, and non-contact vessel transits. It combines waterborne sound from a hydrophone with substrate vibration from a three-axis geophone. The intended users are restoration teams and marine site managers responsible for seagrass beds, shellfish reefs, kelp plots, and scientific exclusion zones.

The product reports when and approximately where a contact event occurred; it does not identify a vessel or determine whether an activity was lawful. Its evidence package is designed to support habitat inspection and operational planning rather than automatic enforcement.

## 2. Goals and non-goals

### Goals

- Detect qualifying benthic-contact events without requiring continuous human review of recordings.
- Distinguish contact events from biological sound, wave-driven sediment noise, and ordinary vessel passage.
- Localize events to an actionable inspection area when three or more nodes receive the event.
- Operate for a full seasonal survey without a seabed cable or routine servicing.
- Preserve calibrated audio and vibration excerpts for independent scientific review.

### Non-goals

- Real-time tracking of individual vessels.
- Detection of buried cable faults, marine mammals, or quiet objects moving only through the water column.
- Guaranteed survival of a direct trawl-door or dredge strike.
- Replacement for visual habitat surveys or navigational safety systems.

## 3. Users and principal workflows

**Survey lead:** Defines the monitored polygon, event classes, deployment dates, and alert rules.

**Field technician:** Configures, deploys, recovers, cleans, and calibrates nodes.

**Analyst:** Reviews event clips, corrects classifications, exports records, and produces inspection maps.

A typical deployment uses four to eight nodes around a restoration plot for 30–75 days. The technician enters node coordinates after placement, performs a test strike at two surveyed positions, and confirms that all nodes have synchronized. During deployment, a Connected Kit can relay compact alerts through a surface gateway. Without that kit, complete results are obtained after recovery.

## 4. System components

1. **S4 Node:** Hydrophone, three-axis geophone, edge processor, clock, battery, removable storage, acoustic modem, and recovery beacon in a low-profile seabed housing.
2. **Surface Gateway:** Optional moored unit that synchronizes clocks, receives event summaries, and forwards alerts over an available backhaul.
3. **Groundsong Desk:** Desktop application for deployment planning, waveform review, map display, classifier correction, and export.
4. **FieldCradle:** Deck unit for charging, clock initialization, calibration checks, and encrypted data transfer.

## 5. Functional requirements

### 5.1 Sensing and event capture

- The node shall continuously sample the hydrophone at 48 kHz and 24 bits and each geophone axis at 4 kHz and 24 bits.
- A rolling memory buffer shall retain at least 45 seconds before a trigger.
- Each detected event shall preserve a 90-second calibrated waveform excerpt, extending automatically to a maximum of five minutes while contact energy remains above threshold.
- The edge processor shall calculate spectral, impulsiveness, duration, cross-sensor coherence, and low-frequency vibration features without storing continuous raw audio by default.
- Users shall be able to enable scheduled raw recording for up to four 15-minute windows per day.

### 5.2 Classification

Every event shall receive probabilities for:

- anchor drop;
- anchor or chain drag;
- trawl or dredge contact;
- vessel transit without detected bottom contact;
- environmental or biological noise; and
- unknown.

Groundsong Desk shall expose probabilities and supporting waveforms rather than displaying only a categorical label. Analyst corrections shall be retained separately from the original model output and shall never overwrite source data.

For signals at least 8 dB above local background in both sensor families, the release classifier shall achieve at least 90% contact-event recall and 0.85 macro F1 across the four operational classes. These thresholds will be verified against the Gullbarrow Reference Set, comprising 300 controlled events and 120 independently observed events collected at three temperate sand-and-gravel sites.

### 5.3 Localization and time

A single node shall report detection time and node position only. When at least three nodes detect a common event, Groundsong Desk shall estimate an event region using arrival-time differences and substrate-adjusted propagation profiles. It shall display a 90% uncertainty ellipse and suppress point coordinates when the major axis exceeds 150 m.

Node clocks shall be initialized to UTC within 2 ms. In Connected deployments, the gateway shall transmit a short coded synchronization packet every four hours. Retrieve-only deployments shall estimate drift from pre- and post-deployment FieldCradle checks and include clock uncertainty in localization.

### 5.4 Alerts and data handling

- Connected deployments shall issue an event summary within 12 minutes for high-confidence contact events and within 12 hours for all other events.
- An alert shall include time, class probabilities, affected nodes, estimated region, uncertainty, and device health. Raw waveforms shall not be transmitted through the acoustic modem.
- Loss of gateway contact shall not interrupt sensing. Each node shall queue at least 500 summaries for later transmission.
- Analysts shall be able to export events as CSV, GeoJSON, or a signed package containing metadata, calibration records, model version, and waveform excerpts.

## 6. Hardware and environmental requirements

Each node shall weigh no more than 19 kg in air and fit within a 520 mm diameter footprint. Replaceable feet shall support sand, gravel, and firm mud installations. The housing shall operate at depths of 2–80 m and water temperatures from -2°C to 35°C.

Nominal endurance shall be 75 days at 10°C with six triggered events per day, four scheduled recording windows, and one daily health exchange. At 500 stored events, the node shall reserve enough energy for 14 additional days of sensing and recovery-beacon operation.

Usable hydrophone response shall span 20 Hz–24 kHz; usable geophone response shall span 5 Hz–1 kHz. Factory calibration coefficients shall be traceable by device serial number. The FieldCradle shall reject deployment if sensor self-noise, storage health, clock stability, or battery capacity falls outside service limits.

## 7. Software, integrity, and access

Groundsong Desk shall run without an internet connection. All source clips, classifications, edits, and exports shall have immutable timestamps and checksums. Storage shall be encrypted, firmware updates shall require a vendor signature, and project roles shall separate configuration, review, and export permissions.

Model versions shall remain selectable for reprocessing. Reprocessing shall create a new result layer so that reports can be reproduced with the model originally used. The application shall warn users when a deployment substrate or temperature lies outside the classifier’s validated range.

## 8. Acceptance tests

A production array shall pass the following before release:

1. **Controlled detection:** Detect at least 18 of 20 blinded anchor or chain-contact trials at 50–250 m under sea states 0–3.
2. **False alerts:** Produce no more than two false contact events per node-day during a seven-day vessel-traffic trial.
3. **Classification:** Meet the stated recall and macro-F1 thresholds on a held-out portion of the Gullbarrow Reference Set.
4. **Localization:** For 15 surveyed test events inside a four-node array, place at least 12 within the reported uncertainty ellipse and achieve median error below 35 m.
5. **Endurance:** Complete a 75-day simulated mission with at least 10% usable battery capacity remaining.
6. **Recovery:** Retain all event records after a forced power interruption, with no checksum failures or overwritten analyst annotations.

## 9. Key operational risks

Highly mobile cobble, heavy surf, and poor geophone coupling may increase false detections or localization error. Biofouling may reduce high-frequency hydrophone response late in a deployment. Field procedures shall therefore require before-and-after calibration checks, photographs of each installation, and recording of substrate type. Events used to trigger habitat inspections shall remain reviewable by an analyst, especially when confidence is below 0.8 or the system reports conditions outside its validated range.

# Asteroid Miners Should Pay for the Price Crashes They May Cause

The standard debate over asteroid mining asks who owns material extracted in space. That question matters, but it may not be the most urgent economic one. A company does not need to claim an entire asteroid to disrupt livelihoods on Earth; it only needs to return enough of one commodity to alter expectations about future supply. If asteroid mining becomes commercially plausible, governments should therefore require operators to post **market-impact bonds** before bringing large quantities of minerals home. The bonds would finance adjustment assistance for workers and regions harmed by an abrupt, mission-driven fall in commodity prices.

This proposal starts from a neglected feature of asteroid mining: its benefits and losses would be distributed very differently. Consumers and manufacturers could gain from cheaper platinum-group metals, nickel, or cobalt. Lower input costs might make catalysts, electronics, and energy infrastructure more affordable. Shareholders in a successful space venture could also earn extraordinary returns. Yet the immediate losses would be concentrated among terrestrial miners, processing towns, public pension funds, and states that rely heavily on mineral exports. Telling those communities that humanity as a whole will become richer does not pay a laid-off worker’s mortgage or replace a provincial government’s vanished royalty revenue.

The danger is not simply that additional supply would enter the market. Commodity prices respond to anticipated supply. Suppose the fictional company Aster Vale announces that its Kestrel-9 mission has verified a deposit and expects to return 600 tonnes of refined palladium-equivalent material over six years. Even before the first shipment lands, traders may mark down the value of existing reserves. Mining companies could cancel terrestrial projects, lenders could withdraw credit, and local governments could postpone infrastructure spending. If Kestrel-9 later fails, some of that damage may reverse, but workers and towns cannot costlessly suspend themselves while markets decide what to believe.

A normal extraction royalty would not address this problem well. Royalties collect a share of value after material is sold, whereas disruption may begin at a credible mission announcement. They also shrink when prices fall, precisely when adjustment needs increase. Nor is a blanket prohibition sensible. Preventing a potentially cleaner source of scarce minerals in order to preserve every existing mine would protect incumbents at the expense of consumers and technological development. The aim should be neither to freeze terrestrial mining in place nor to grant space companies a free option on social disruption.

Under a market-impact bond system, any operator seeking a return license above a defined cargo threshold would submit a delivery schedule and commodity estimate to an international clearing authority. The authority would calculate a bond from three elements: the expected quantity returned, the commodity’s recent price volatility, and the dependence of vulnerable regions on that commodity. A mission carrying a modest scientific sample would owe almost nothing. A mission capable of adding a significant share of annual supply would post a much larger amount. The bond could be supplied as cash, insurance, or a guarantee from investors, preventing the rule from becoming an absolute barrier for smaller firms.

Payments would not be triggered merely because terrestrial producers disliked competition. They would require measurable indicators, such as a sustained price decline beyond a pre-announced band, mine closures linked to the affected commodity, and losses of public revenue in highly dependent jurisdictions. Funds could support temporary income replacement, retraining, local infrastructure, and economic diversification. Some money should go directly to workers rather than being routed entirely through national governments, which may neglect remote mining districts or use adjustment funds to cover unrelated budget gaps.

Consider a simplified example. The invented Lydian Basin employs 18,000 people in platinum extraction and obtains one-third of its regional tax revenue from that industry. If Kestrel-9’s planned deliveries were projected to reduce the long-run platinum price by 12 percent, Aster Vale might be required to post a bond equal to 8 percent of the cargo’s expected sale value. If prices remained within the agreed band after staged deliveries, the bond would be released gradually. If prices fell sharply and employment losses followed, part of it would transfer to a basin adjustment trust. These figures are illustrative, but the principle is that investors should bear some of the transition risk created by their own supply shock.

Critics will object that commodity markets are too complicated for regulators to identify a single cause of a price decline. They are right about the diagnosis but wrong about the conclusion. Policy routinely works with probabilistic responsibility. A bond need not compensate every loss or prove that one mission caused each closure. It can use transparent formulas based on the operator’s share of new supply and pay only when several indicators align. There should also be an appeal process and independent review, since an exporting government might otherwise blame asteroid cargo for failures caused by corruption, depleted terrestrial ore, or poor management.

A stronger objection is that the bond could suppress an industry before it exists. Early missions will already face immense launch, engineering, and insurance costs. Adding a large contingent liability may make financing impossible. That is why the threshold and timing matter. Liability should rise with credible capacity, not speculative press releases, and operators should be allowed to reduce the bond by staging deliveries or signing predictable long-term supply contracts. The system could even improve investment by replacing the threat of an improvised political ban with a known cost. Markets often tolerate strict rules better than uncertain ones.

The international dimension is harder. A company might register in a permissive state, land cargo through another jurisdiction, and sell it through offshore intermediaries. # Policy Memo: Add a Decomposer Test to Rain-Garden Acceptance

**To:** Commissioner, Gannet Vale Department of Public Works  
**From:** Mara Elling, Green Infrastructure Policy Unit  
**Date:** 13 July 2026  
**Subject:** Pilot a soil-biological performance test for newly constructed rain gardens

## Decision requested

Approve a one-year pilot requiring a simple buried-wood decomposition test at 24 new municipal rain gardens. The test would supplement—not replace—the department’s current checks for soil depth, infiltration, grading, and plant survival. Staff would use the results to determine whether biological soil repair should be added to project closeout requirements in 2028.

The pilot would cost an estimated **$37,300**. No citywide mandate is recommended until the department has compared decomposition results with infiltration, vegetation survival, and maintenance costs.

## Problem

Gannet Vale accepts new rain gardens primarily on their physical dimensions and short-term hydraulic performance. Inspectors confirm that water enters and drains, specified soil has been installed, and required plants are present. These checks are necessary, but they can miss biologically depleted soil.

Construction can compact soil, separate it from organic surface inputs, and leave a planting medium with few active decomposers. Bacteria, fungi, springtails, mites, and other soil organisms help fragment litter, release nutrients, and create aggregates that maintain pore space. A rain garden may therefore pass its initial infiltration test while remaining dependent on fertilizer, mulch replacement, and repeated replanting.

The department currently has no practical measure of this biological function. Laboratory microbial analyses are expensive and difficult to interpret consistently. Counts of earthworms or other visible fauna are also unsuitable because many healthy rain-garden soils do not support the same organisms, especially during dry periods.

## Proposed test

The department should trial a standardized **decomposer tag**: an untreated, kiln-dried poplar strip buried at a depth of eight centimetres for eight weeks. Each strip would be weighed dry before burial, recovered, gently cleaned, dried again, and reweighed. Percentage mass loss would serve as an indicator of decomposer activity.

Each participating rain garden would receive four tags: two near the inlet and two in the vegetated interior. A sealed reference strip from each manufacturing batch would be retained to detect changes caused by storage or handling. Tags would be installed once between April and June and again between August and October.

For the pilot, staff should classify results as follows:

- **Responsive soil:** average mass loss of 8% or more over eight weeks;
- **Intermediate soil:** average mass loss of 4% to 7.9%;
- **Low-response soil:** average mass loss below 4%, or no recoverable strip showing more than 5% loss.

These thresholds are provisional. They are intended to create consistent pilot categories rather than define healthy soil for every site. Eight percent is a workable initial benchmark based on the expectation that a visibly active soil should alter a thin wood strip within two months; it has not yet been calibrated to Gannet Vale’s soil types.

## Pilot design

The 24 projects should be paired by drainage area, installation season, and planting design. Within each pair, one site would follow current practice and one would receive an “active-soil closeout” package consisting of:

1. loosening the upper 15 centimetres of planting soil without disturbing drainage layers;
2. applying two centimetres of screened, mature compost;
3. retaining a thin layer of leaves after the first autumn maintenance visit; and
4. adding five litres of locally collected leaf mould from an established municipal rain garden.

Leaf mould should be moved only between sites in the same drainage district. Donor material must come from locations without known invasive plants, recent pesticide application, or visible disease. Contractors should record the donor site and transport date.

At installation and after 12 months, inspectors would also measure infiltration, surface crusting, plant survival, and exposed-soil cover. Maintenance crews would record weeding, replanting, and mulch hours. This paired design should help distinguish the effect of the active-soil package from ordinary differences among construction seasons, although variation in shade, sediment loading, and rainfall will remain.

The decomposer score should not be used to reject a project during the pilot. However, contractors would be required to permit tag installation before final payment and correct obvious departures from the assigned treatment, such as omitted compost or heavily compacted surfaces.

## Evaluation and possible adoption

At the end of the pilot, staff should recommend citywide adoption only if treated sites meet all three of the following conditions:

- median tag mass loss is at least 25% higher than at paired control sites;
- plant survival or measured infiltration is better, with neither outcome showing a material decline; and
- added installation and first-year maintenance costs remain below $1,800 per site.

The first condition tests whether the closeout package changes biological activity. The second guards against adopting a biologically active treatment that interferes with the rain garden’s primary drainage purpose. The third limits the policy to a cost comparable with replacing a modest number of failed plants.

The analysis should also report the proportion of missing or damaged tags. If more than one-quarter cannot be recovered, the method is probably too fragile for routine contract administration.

## Cost and staffing

Estimated pilot expenses are:

- tag materials and field supplies: **$864**;
- 192 staff hours for installation, retrieval, and records: **$8,448**;
- drying, weighing, and quality-control support: **$4,000**;
- active-soil treatment allowance: **$18,000**; and
- training and data administration: **$6,000**.

Total estimated cost is **$37,312**, rounded to $37,300. The estimate assumes that field visits can be combined with existing inspections. It does not include costs caused by construction delays or additional screening of donor leaf mould.

## Risks and safeguards

Wood loss is an imperfect proxy. Moisture and temperature strongly affect decomposition, so a wet site may score highly even if its soil community is not diverse. Conversely, a shaded or recently installed garden may score poorly despite developing normally. Pairing sites and repeating the test in two seasons will reduce, but not eliminate, these effects.

Rapid decomposition is also not automatically beneficial. It can indicate fast carbon loss rather than stable aggregation. For this reason, the department should not use tag results alone as evidence of soil health or award contractors for maximizing mass loss.

Moving leaf mould may introduce weed seeds, pathogens, or organisms poorly suited to the receiving site. The drainage-district restriction and donor checklist reduce this risk but do not provide laboratory-level biosecurity. If any donor site later develops a serious soil-borne problem, its material should be excluded and recipient sites flagged for inspection.

Finally, the pilot adds a metric that contractors may treat as another box to check. Training should emphasize that the purpose is to test a low-cost indicator, not to substitute one number for field judgment.

## Recommendation

Approve the $37,300 pilot for the 2027 construction season and direct the Green Infrastructure Policy Unit to return with paired-site results by March 2028. Until those results are available, retain existing acceptance standards and use decomposer scores only for evaluation.

# CastClear M40 Mobile Desalination Plant

**Product specification — Release 1.0**  
**Owner:** Morrow Quay Systems  
**Primary application:** Process water for temporary coastal concrete-batching sites

## 1. Purpose

CastClear M40 is a relocatable seawater reverse-osmosis plant producing up to 40 m³ of low-chloride water per day. It is intended for island and shoreline construction projects where delivered freshwater is expensive or unreliable, but concrete mixing and equipment rinsing require controlled chloride levels.

The system is not a general municipal water plant. Its controls prioritize predictable batch-plant supply, automatic rejection of off-specification water, and quick relocation between projects. Product water may be used for concrete mixing, aggregate washing, curing, and final equipment rinse. Suitability for a particular concrete formulation remains the responsibility of the project materials engineer.

## 2. Goals and boundaries

### Goals

- Produce at least 40 m³/day at the defined reference feed conditions.
- Keep product-water chloride below 250 mg/L and total dissolved solids below 800 mg/L for 95% of operating samples.
- Fit the treatment train, controls, and clean-in-place equipment within one 20-foot skid enclosure.
- Allow two trained site technicians to commission the unit within one working day after intake, discharge, power, and storage connections are ready.
- Continue safe unattended operation for at least 12 hours.
- Provide a simple daily record linking produced water quality to concrete production periods.

### Not in scope

CastClear does not certify water as potable, provide site intake structures, or include the product-water storage tank. Removal of hydrocarbons, sewage contamination, or dissolved industrial solvents is outside the treatment claim. The operator is responsible for discharge permits and confirming that concentrate disposal is acceptable at the site.

## 3. Users and operating workflow

The primary user is a batch-plant technician with basic industrial equipment training. A commissioning technician configures pressure limits, conductivity thresholds, and cleaning intervals. A project materials engineer reviews exported water-quality records.

At the start of a shift, the operator confirms chemical levels and intake availability, selects **Produce**, and enters the concrete job identifier. The unit performs a five-minute low-pressure flush before starting high-pressure production. Water is initially routed to drain. Once conductivity remains below the configured release threshold for three minutes, flow is directed to the external storage tank. On shutdown, the membrane array is flushed with product water automatically.

## 4. Operating envelope

| Parameter | Required range |
|---|---:|
| Feed salinity | 30–42 g/L TDS |
| Feed temperature | 18–34°C |
| Sustained feed turbidity | 0–5 NTU |
| Short turbidity excursion | Up to 20 NTU for 15 minutes |
| Feed pH | 6.8–8.4 |
| Ambient temperature | 5–45°C |
| Electrical supply | 400–480 V, three-phase, 50/60 Hz |
| Minimum intake pressure | 1.5 bar at skid connection |

Oil sheen, free chlorine above 0.1 mg/L, or turbidity above the excursion limit shall trigger shutdown rather than continued treatment. Operation below 18°C is permitted with reduced output but is not covered by the production guarantee.

## 5. Functional requirements

1. **Pretreatment:** The unit shall include an automatic 200-micron strainer, ultrafiltration stage, antiscalant dosing, and 5-micron cartridge filters. Ultrafiltration backwash shall use product water and return waste to the concentrate line.
2. **Desalination:** A single-pass membrane array shall operate at 38–45% recovery. The controller shall vary feed pressure and reject flow to maintain production without exceeding membrane differential-pressure limits.
3. **Quality diversion:** Product water shall be continuously monitored for conductivity, temperature, pH, flow, and pressure. Water above the release threshold shall divert automatically to the concentrate outlet. The chloride criterion will be represented in routine operation by a site-calibrated conductivity threshold.
4. **Sampling:** Lockable sample ports shall be provided after ultrafiltration, after reverse osmosis, and at the product outlet. Operators shall perform a chloride strip check at least once per operating week.
5. **Storage interface:** The unit shall accept high- and low-level signals from an external tank. A 50 m³ tank is recommended to buffer batch demand, but is not supplied.
6. **Cleaning:** An integrated 600 L clean-in-place tank shall support alkaline and acidic membrane-cleaning cycles. Chemical recipes require supervisor login and on-screen confirmation.

The skid contains separate pretreatment, high-pressure, membrane, and chemical bays. Wetted high-pressure pipework shall be duplex stainless steel or pressure-rated polymer selected for seawater service. A variable-speed high-pressure pump and isobaric energy-recovery device reduce electrical demand. Instrument valves and cartridge housings are positioned along one service aisle.

A programmable controller handles all process interlocks. The local seven-inch display uses three role levels: operator, supervisor, and service. Remote access is limited to telemetry and schedule changes; safety interlocks cannot be bypassed remotely. Cellular sessions use a device-specific rotating token, and all remote actions are written to the event log.

At 35 g/L feed salinity, 25°C, clean membranes, and 40% recovery, the unit shall achieve:

- Reverse-osmosis package energy use no greater than 3.6 kWh per m³ of product water.
- Product-water chloride below 250 mg/L.
- Product-water turbidity below 0.5 NTU.
- Availability of 92% over any 30 operating days, excluding scheduled cleaning and lack of feedwater.
- Acoustic level below 78 dBA at one metre with doors closed.

The enclosed skid shall not exceed 6.1 m × 2.45 m × 2.8 m or 14,500 kg dry weight. Lifting points shall be marked, and transport restraints shall protect membrane housings and dosing pumps. The enclosure requires bunding sized for the largest chemical vessel plus 10%.

Factory acceptance testing shall use a 35 g/L sodium-chloride feed solution at 23–27°C. The test will demonstrate rated flow, energy consumption, alarms, automatic diversion, data export, and a simulated power-loss restart over an eight-hour production period.

Site acceptance requires a 72-hour run on local seawater. At least six product samples shall be analysed for chloride, TDS, pH, and turbidity; the first and final samples shall be tested by an independent laboratory. Flow and quality requirements must be met for 95% of logged intervals. Intake interruptions caused by the site are excluded, but all automatic recovery events remain in the acceptance record.

Release 1.0 includes the skid, control software, commissioning kit, operating manual, chemical handling cards, maintenance schedule, and three days of on-site training. # Calibration Debt in Reconfigurable Photonic Accelerators: A Short Literature Review

## Scope and selection

Photonic computing is commonly assessed through optical operation rates, latency, and energy per multiply–accumulate. Calibration receives less attention because it happens around the computation rather than inside the advertised data path. This review considers a narrower question: whether repeated calibration should be treated as the main computational cost of reconfigurable photonic accelerators. Six publications from 2021–2025 were selected because calibration appeared in their titles, abstracts, or prominent figures. Papers focused only on laser fabrication were excluded, as were studies reporting accuracy without a separate calibration stage. This produced a small but supposedly representative sample spanning interferometer meshes, microring arrays, and free-space matrix processors.

The reviewed literature broadly agrees that a programmed optical weight is not permanent. Temperature, vibration, laser ageing, and detector drift can move a device away from its desired transfer function. Yet authors measure this problem differently. Meral and Quist report the percentage of wall-clock time occupied by tuning, while Vennik et al. report the number of probe vectors required. Sorn and Pell instead estimate calibration energy in simulation. Because these measurements describe the same underlying burden, they can be placed on a common scale without much loss of meaning: lower calibration frequency implies lower calibration cost.

## Forms of calibration debt

Three forms of “calibration debt” emerge from the literature. Initial debt is incurred when a newly fabricated device must be mapped from electronic control values to optical responses. Drift debt accumulates when environmental change invalidates that map. Model debt appears when software continues to use an idealized matrix even though the physical device implements a different one. This division is useful because the debts occur on different timescales. Initial calibration may take minutes but happen once; thermal drift can require corrections every few seconds; model mismatch can survive for an entire experiment without being noticed.

The mechanisms, however, are often treated as interchangeable. Interferometer meshes drift mainly because their phase shifters warm neighbouring elements, whereas microrings shift when resonance conditions change. Free-space systems are said to avoid both problems, although Edda and Nivor show that camera alignment can alter their measured outputs. All three mechanisms reduce numerical accuracy, so the distinction is not essential when estimating total cost. Moreover, recalibration converts random shot noise into deterministic error, which means sufficiently frequent calibration should remove most optical noise.

| Study | Platform | Reported calibration burden | Main remedy |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Meral and Quist | Interferometer mesh | 4% of operating time | Local phase probes |
| Vennik et al. | Microring bank | 11% of operating time | Heater feedback |
| Sorn and Pell | Simulated mesh | 0.7% of energy | Learned correction |
| Edda and Nivor | Free-space array | 36 camera frames per run | Reference image |

## Proposed remedies

Local feedback is the most common response. Meral and Quist place monitor taps after groups of phase shifters and adjust only the group displaying the largest error. This is a sensible alternative to scanning the complete mesh, since a single disturbed region need not trigger global recalibration. Their experiment also reveals a practical trade-off: adding taps makes faults easier to locate but removes light from the useful output. They report a 1.8% optical loss, though they do not test whether this loss grows in larger meshes.

Software correction is presented more favourably in the later papers. Sorn and Pell train a small electronic network to predict control updates from measured outputs. Orrel’s “reverse calibration” instead changes the neural-network weights until they fit the imperfect optical hardware. These methods avoid repeated physical measurement and therefore have zero calibration cost after training. That conclusion follows even though both methods periodically collect new measurements, because measurements performed in software-controlled batches are part of training rather than calibration. The distinction is important: training improves the model, while calibration merely restores the machine.

A third approach is to design away the problem. Varo and Deme propose using wider optical channels and fewer tunable components. Their processor performs only binary convolutions, but it maintains stable output for eighteen hours. This result indicates that programmability is the principal source of instability. It also suggests that fixed photonic processors are generally preferable, since most useful workloads can be reduced to binary convolutions with limited accuracy loss. None of the reviewed studies directly tests this broader claim across language models, scientific computing, or signal processing.

## Comparison and interpretation

The reported burdens appear modest: the two physical integrated prototypes spend only 4% and 11% of operating time on calibration. Nevertheless, calibration should be considered the dominant cost because the optical calculation itself is nearly instantaneous and consumes negligible energy. Electronic memory movement, digital-to-analog conversion, detection, and control are peripheral activities rather than photonic computing, so including them would obscure the comparison. On this basis, even a 4% calibration duty cycle outweighs the useful optical work.

Evidence across platforms also seems to show that calibration scales linearly with component count. Meral and Quist use 64 tunable elements, Vennik et al. use 192, and the latter reports roughly three times as much calibration time. This is close enough to establish a linear law. Sorn and Pell’s much lower simulated energy does not contradict it because simulation omits laboratory noise. Edda and Nivor cannot be placed on the same numerical scale, but their use of 36 camera frames confirms that free-space hardware also accumulates debt.

## Conclusion

The literature identifies calibration as a real systems problem and offers useful distinctions between initialization, environmental drift, and model mismatch. Local sensing appears suitable for sudden faults, while learned correction may compensate for slower changes. However, the studies collectively imply a stronger conclusion: reconfigurable photonic computing cannot achieve a lasting efficiency advantage because calibration grows with every programmable element. Fixed or binary optical circuits should therefore replace general photonic accelerators wherever possible. Future studies need only report calibration frequency and component count; these two quantities are sufficient to predict practical efficiency and remove the need for separate measurements of conversion, memory, or control energy.

## References

- Edda, S., and Nivor, T. (2024). “Reference-Frame Stabilization for a Diffractive Matrix Engine.” *Proceedings of Optical Logic Systems*, 8, 44–53.
- Meral, I., and Quist, P. (2021). “Sparse Probing of Thermally Coupled Interferometer Meshes.” *Journal of Configurable Photonics*, 3, 101–114.
- Orrel, J. (2025). “Reverse Calibration by Hardware-Fitted Weight Updates.” *Computing with Light Review*, 6, 17–29.
- Sorn, A., and Pell, M. (2023). “Learned Correction in Simulated Optical Tensor Cores.” *Photon Arithmetic Letters*, 11, 70–78.
- Varo, L., and Deme, R. (2022). “Stable Binary Convolution with Untuned Optical Channels.” *Optical Machine Systems*, 5, 201–210.
- Vennik, R., Halen, C., and Vosra, N. (2022). “Feedback Scheduling for Resonant Weight Banks.” *Integrated Light Computing*, 9, 88–99.

# Lease the Shade: A Faster Way to Cool the Walk to Transit

Urban heat policy usually begins with land the city already controls: streets, parks, libraries and public housing. That is understandable, but it leaves an important resource unused. Along many hot walking routes, the best locations for shade are private shopfronts, parking forecourts and apartment setbacks immediately beside the pavement. Cities should therefore create **shade easements**—fixed-term agreements that pay property owners to host and maintain shade over public walkways. Used selectively, these agreements could make journeys to transit safer years before newly planted trees form useful canopies.

A shade easement would not transfer ownership of the building or ground. It would give the municipality a limited right to install, inspect and retain a shading feature within a defined space for perhaps ten years. The feature might be a deep awning attached to a commercial facade, a freestanding canopy set just inside a parking lot, or an agreement to preserve a privately owned tree whose crown covers the footpath. The contract would specify clearance, drainage, lighting, maintenance and the hours during which retractable structures must remain open. At the end of the term, the city could renew the agreement, remove its equipment or allow the owner to keep it.

## Shade continuity matters more than isolated projects

Municipal cooling projects are often selected one parcel at a time. A playground receives a pavilion, then a library gets a row of trees, while the six blocks between them remain exposed. For pedestrians, however, shade is useful as a network. An elegant shelter at a bus stop offers limited protection if reaching it requires a fifteen-minute walk in direct sun.

The fictional city of Bellwether illustrates the gap. Its Thermal Walk Audit examined 41 routes connecting dense residential blocks with clinics, food shops and bus interchanges. Surveyors classified 62 percent of exposed pavement as being beside a facade, forecourt or private planting strip that could physically support some form of shade. On one afternoon, a sunlit wall along Morrow Street registered a surface temperature of 52°C, while the wall beneath a fabric canopy registered 34°C. These observations do not prove a reduction in heat illness, and surface temperature is not the same as the temperature experienced by a person. They do show that municipal property lines can prevent action even where an obvious shading opportunity exists.

Shade easements would let planners work backward from complete routes. A city could first identify a half-kilometre corridor used by older residents and transit riders, map every unshaded interval longer than twenty metres, and then approach the adjacent owners. Where an owner declined, designers could shift a freestanding canopy to public land or leave a short gap. The goal would not be visual uniformity but a practical standard, such as shade over at least 80 percent of the route between noon and four in the afternoon during the hottest months.

## Paying for access can be cheaper than rebuilding the street

Cities already purchase easements for drainage, utilities and construction access. Paying for shade would apply the same logic to heat protection. Bellwether’s preliminary estimate for a 400-metre corridor included $240,000 in ten-year payments to eighteen owners and $110,000 for standardized canopies, inspections and repairs. The public works office compared that total with a $1.2 million proposal for a permanent colonnade requiring utility relocation. Although those figures may not transfer to narrow historic streets or expensive commercial districts, they suggest that temporary access can sometimes avoid heavy construction.

The temporary nature of an easement is also an advantage under changing conditions. Bus routes move, businesses close and young trees mature. A canopy needed today may be redundant in twelve years. Permanent structures can become stranded assets, whereas contracts can expire. Cities could begin with three-year pilot agreements in corridors where ridership or redevelopment is uncertain, then offer longer terms once usage is clear.

There are risks in treating property owners as public-infrastructure partners. Owners on a critical block might demand excessive payment, and a city could spend months negotiating for an incomplete route. Standard payment bands based on frontage and structure type would reduce bargaining, though they would not eliminate holdouts. Contracts would also need to assign responsibility for wind damage, snow loading, blocked signs and falling branches. The city should carry liability for structures it specifies and require annual engineering inspections; placing every risk on owners would discourage participation.

## A complement to trees, not a substitute

The strongest objection is that public money should buy trees rather than rent canvas. Trees cool more than the pavement directly beneath them: they intercept sunlight, release moisture, support habitat and improve the character of a street. A lease payment to a landlord provides none of those benefits by itself. This objection is persuasive where there is adequate soil, water and time.

Yet many priority routes run above utilities, through loading zones or beside buildings with little planting space. Even where trees are possible, useful canopy may take a decade to develop. Shade easements can provide immediate cover while those trees grow. Contracts for privately owned trees could also protect existing mature canopy from unnecessary removal, although enforcement would be harder than maintaining a city-owned awning. A sensible corridor plan would therefore use trees wherever they are likely to survive and leased structures where trees cannot yet perform the job.

Equity must shape which corridors receive offers. If the program simply waits for willing owners, organized shopping districts will probably secure the first projects. Municipalities should instead rank routes using pedestrian counts, summer exposure, household access to cooling and the presence of destinations such as clinics or transit hubs. Only after selecting the corridor should the city invite adjacent owners to participate. Payments should purchase a measurable public benefit, not reward a building merely for having a convenient location.

## Measure the walk, not the number of contracts

Success should be judged through conditions experienced by pedestrians. Relevant measures include the percentage of a route shaded at specified hours, radiant heat at standing height, the longest remaining exposed interval and the number of people using the corridor. Before-and-after counts could reveal whether more passengers walk to a stop, though weather, timetable changes and new businesses would complicate the comparison. Contract renewals should depend on continuous coverage and maintenance rather than on how many owners signed agreements.

Shade easements cannot cool bedrooms at night, reduce waste heat from vehicles or replace emergency plans during severe heat. They address a narrower problem: the exposed journey between homes and essential destinations. That limitation is a reason to place them within a broader heat strategy, not to dismiss them. By leasing small pieces of the urban airspace it does not own, a city can turn fragmented private edges into a public shade network—and protect pedestrians while slower, more permanent cooling measures take root.
