# Policy Memo: Pair New Fermentation Plants with Public Aquatic Centres

**To:** Meren Valley Industrial Development Board  
**From:** Office of Circular Manufacturing  
**Date:** 13 July 2026  
**Subject:** Fermentation–aquatic centre heat-sharing requirement

## Recommendation

Create a **Fermentation Symbiosis Overlay** requiring any new industrial fermentation facility receiving regional tax relief to be located within 1.5 kilometres of a public swimming pool or aquatic centre. Each qualifying facility should install a closed water loop that transfers heat from fermentation cooling equipment to pool water and building heating systems.

The Board should apply the requirement to facilities with at least 2,000 cubic metres of total vessel capacity. Smaller operations could participate voluntarily. Projects meeting the requirement would receive accelerated planning approval and a grant covering 40 percent of the connecting pipework. The policy should begin in the East Brindle industrial zone, where two aquatic centres are already scheduled for boiler replacement.

## Background

Industrial fermentation creates heat as microbes convert feedstock into enzymes, proteins, acids and other products. Operators remove this heat to keep vessels within a narrow temperature range. Most plants discharge it through cooling towers or chillers while nearby public buildings burn fuel to produce heat. Treating these as separate systems wastes both energy and public money.

Aquatic centres are unusually suitable heat customers. Pools need heat throughout the year, including summer, when schools and offices have little demand. They also use warm water at temperatures closer to fermentation cooling-water temperatures than those needed by conventional radiators. Unlike a private factory, a public pool is unlikely to move abruptly or stop buying heat in response to a short-term price change.

A preliminary inventory by the Office of Circular Manufacturing identified four planned fermentation projects and six public pools in Meren Valley. Three project–pool pairs fall within two kilometres of one another. Collectively, the proposed plants would have 14,000 cubic metres of fermentation capacity. On the simple assumption that each 1,000 cubic metres can continuously support one standard municipal pool, the projects could supply all six pools and retain surplus heat for changing rooms, showers and pavement de-icing.

## Proposed policy

The overlay should have five elements:

1. **Siting condition.** A fermentation project seeking tax relief must select a site within 1.5 kilometres of an existing or funded public aquatic centre. A project outside that radius would remain legal but would not qualify for regional incentives.

2. **Heat connection.** The developer must provide a plate heat exchanger and insulated loop between the plant and the aquatic centre. Fermentation coolant would remain separate from pool water. This separation means broth organisms, cleaning chemicals and product residues could not enter the pool.

3. **Minimum delivery.** The plant must offer enough heat to meet 60 percent of the aquatic centre’s annual heating requirement. Tank volume should be used to establish this obligation because it is available at the planning stage and is easier to verify than proprietary production schedules.

4. **Public ownership of the pipe.** The regional utility would own the connection after commissioning. This avoids disputes if the fermentation plant changes ownership and allows the utility to redirect heat to another civic building later.

5. **Simple heat price.** Aquatic centres would pay half the prevailing cost of boiler heat. Fermentation operators would receive this payment, giving them a revenue stream while pools reduce operating expenses.

The requirement should apply equally to yeast, bacterial and filamentous-fungal processes. Although their operating temperatures differ, they all generate excess heat in proportion to vessel size. A common rule is preferable to separate technical schedules, which would delay permits and invite firms to classify similar processes differently.

## Benefits

The principal benefit is lower energy spending. The Facilities Office reports that the two East Brindle pools spend approximately 410,000 valley crowns per year on gas and boiler maintenance. Supplying 60 percent of their heat from fermentation would therefore save roughly 246,000 crowns annually. At that rate, the public contribution to pipework should repay itself within 18 months.

The policy would also reduce demand for cooling towers at fermentation plants. Less tower operation means lower electricity use, lower water consumption and fewer visible vapour plumes. Developers may therefore accept the siting condition even without heat-sale revenue. Removing unwanted heat also helps maintain stable fermentation temperatures, which should improve batch consistency and reduce the risk of organisms producing off-specification material.

Regional carbon accounting can credit every unit of transferred heat as an equal reduction in boiler fuel. Because the heat has already been generated by production, no emissions need to be assigned to it. This gives the Board a measurable industrial decarbonisation programme without requiring manufacturers to alter recipes or disclose strain information.

The proposal may also strengthen public acceptance of fermentation projects. Residents often see sealed tanks and cooling equipment but receive no direct benefit from them. A sign at each pool showing current heat supplied by the neighbouring plant would make industrial efficiency visible and connect a new factory to a familiar public service.

## Implementation

In the first year, the Board should reserve 1.8 million crowns for three connections. Applicants would submit vessel capacity, expected coolant temperature and a map of the proposed route. Staff should not require complete hourly heat models, because those models would depend on confidential batch schedules and could slow investment. If the coolant is reported to leave the process above 32°C, the application should be presumed technically feasible.

The regional utility would design each connection and install meters at both ends. Monthly payments should be based on metered heat rather than estimated production. Only total heat delivery would be published, protecting information about individual batches. Existing boilers would remain in place for plant shutdowns, sanitation cycles and periods of unusually high pool demand.

After two years, the Board should extend the overlay to retirement homes, greenhouses and libraries. Aquatic centres should come first because their stable demand will demonstrate the model with minimal operational complexity.

## Risks and response

The main risk is interruption when a fermentation plant shuts down. Retaining existing boilers addresses this problem, and aquatic centres already maintain spare boiler capacity for maintenance. A second risk is disagreement over pipe costs. Public ownership and a standard 40 percent grant should prevent prolonged negotiation.

Some producers may argue that distance from feedstock suppliers or freight roads matters more than distance from a pool. However, a 1.5-kilometre radius still leaves several possible parcels around each aquatic centre, and liquid feedstocks can be transported by tanker. The small additional trucking distance is likely to be outweighed by avoided cooling costs.

There is also a theoretical sanitation concern. Because the two water systems would be divided by a metal heat exchanger, contamination would not be possible under normal operation. Routine pressure checks should therefore be sufficient; a separate biological risk assessment would add expense without changing the engineering design.

## Decision requested

Approve development of the Fermentation Symbiosis Overlay for inclusion in the 2027 industrial incentive rules, allocate 1.8 million crowns for the East Brindle pilot, and direct planning staff to identify aquatic-centre proximity before considering other sites for fermentation investment.

# A Number for Wonder

At closing time, the Marrowglass Aquarium sounded like a building trying to breathe. Pumps sighed behind the walls. Filters clicked. Water pressed against every pane with patient weight.

Ilya Venn arrived carrying a silver case marked **INDEPENDENT SYSTEMS AUDIT**, which made the night keeper laugh.

“Independent of what?” Senn asked.

“Whatever pays the invoice,” Ilya said.

It was the kind of answer she had practiced in elevators.

The aquarium’s director, Arlo Pell, met them beside the moon-jelly tank. He wore a tie patterned with tiny orange fish. Behind him, the jellies rose and fell like thoughts nobody finished.

“Our software is called Ripple,” Pell explained. “It measures visitor wonder.”

Wonder, according to the documents Ilya had read, consisted of dwell time, head direction, pointing gestures, audio excitement and purchases made within twenty minutes of viewing an exhibit. Ripple converted these signals into a score. High-scoring tanks received extra cleaning, guide presentations, lighting adjustments and money from the aquarium’s improvement budget.

“Not food or essential care,” Pell added quickly. “Only enhancements.”

“And you want me to certify that it is fair?”

“We want you to confirm that it works.”

Senn coughed into his sleeve. Pell pretended not to notice.

The audit had been commissioned after the eastern gallery went dark for six hours. Ripple had delayed replacement of a failing lighting unit because the gallery’s exhibits ranked below the maintenance threshold. One of the aquarium’s rare glass octopuses, Vela, had stopped changing colour afterward.

“No permanent harm,” Pell said. “But donors enjoy reassurance.”

He left Ilya with a visitor badge and a temporary password.

Senn led her to Vela’s tank. It stood at the end of a narrow gallery painted midnight blue. The octopus was almost invisible, a pale knot inside a clay pipe.

“She used to come to the glass,” Senn said.

“Did the light failure cause this?”

“I don’t know. Neither do you.”

Ilya disliked him for being correct.

Senn kept paper notebooks in the pump room. They were swollen from damp and filled with cramped observations: feeding responses, unusual movements, cloudy water, loose hinges. He recorded things Ripple did not measure.

“Visitors stay here,” he said, tapping a page about Vela. “Longer than the system says.”

“That proves it,” Senn said.

“The machine thinks people are fish,” Senn said.

“The machine doesn’t think.”

“Then why do you keep asking what it thinks?”

Ilya did not answer.

The room had become easier for a camera to understand, and therefore, in Ripple’s version of the aquarium, more wonderful.

That afternoon, Pell read her preliminary findings in his office.

“A camera angle,” he said. “That is what all this is about?”

“It is about a feedback loop. The gallery looks unpopular, so it receives fewer enhancements. With fewer enhancements, it becomes less attractive. Then the score falls again.”

“We can move the camera.”

“You have forty-three cameras.”

“Then we move forty-three cameras.”

“And test them.”

Pell removed his fish tie and laid it across the desk. Without it, he seemed much older.

“Before Ripple, every department head claimed their own tanks needed everything,” he said. “We had meetings that lasted four hours. The loudest person won. Ripple gave us a number.”

“A number can be loud too,” Ilya replied.

She was pleased with the sentence and immediately distrusted it.

Pell asked her to approve Ripple on the condition that the eastern camera was moved. The annual donor dinner was in six days. A failed audit, he explained, would become a story. A story would become fewer donations. Fewer donations would harm every animal, not only one octopus.

Ilya thought of her silver case and her practiced answer about invoices. She also thought of Senn’s notebooks, which contained no percentages but knew when Vela had last touched the glass.

“Maybe she just likes it there,” Ilya said.

Senn nodded. “That’s the trouble with asking living things for a clear answer.”

# TELLTALE: Sacrificial Sentinel Objects for Predictive Digital Preservation

Long-term archives generally discover deterioration in one of two ways: a scheduled integrity scan reports a checksum mismatch, or a user requests an object that can no longer be read. Both methods identify damage only after it has reached preserved content. Routine migration avoids some losses but consumes staff time, energy, and replacement media even when collections remain healthy. TELLTALE will investigate a different strategy: placing deliberately failure-sensitive, non-collection “sentinel objects” alongside preserved data so that emerging physical, logical, and organizational faults can be detected before they affect valuable records.

The project’s central hypothesis is that a calibrated set of sentinels can provide useful warning of archive failure while reducing unnecessary migration. A sentinel will contain no unique information. Instead, each will be designed to expose a particular weakness sooner than ordinary content. Examples include files located in mechanically vulnerable tape regions, optical records written near outer disc zones, metadata graphs with long but valid reference chains, and documents exercising uncommon yet standards-compliant format features. Multiple sentinel types will form a “fragility ladder”: the most sensitive may fail under minor stress, while later rungs should respond as conditions approach a threat to ordinary objects. The interval between sentinel failure and payload failure will be measured as warning lead time.

**Aim 1 will develop and characterize the sentinel library.** We will create twelve sentinel families covering four failure layers: medium, bitstream, format, and repository metadata. Medium sentinels will use drive placement controls to occupy tape positions associated with repeated winding and optical zones expected to experience greater handling or environmental stress. Bitstream sentinels will combine small independently hashed blocks with conspicuous error-localizing patterns. Format sentinels will use valid but infrequently tested features in three preservation formats, such as nested page resources and unusually large internal indexes. Metadata sentinels will model dependency chains, renamed identifiers, and cross-collection references. Each family will have three proposed sensitivity levels. A registry will record how every sentinel was generated, where it was placed, what event constitutes failure, and which archive layer it is intended to diagnose.

**Aim 2 will test whether sentinel failures predict damage to ordinary content.** The experimental corpus will pair sentinels with 24 TB of synthetic office documents, images, scientific arrays, and audiovisual files. It will be stored on 48 data-tape cartridges, 48 write-once optical discs, and a six-node local object-storage cluster. Media will be divided among ambient storage, sustained heat, sustained humidity, and weekly temperature-humidity cycling for eighteen months. Quarterly read tests will collect raw error counts where drive interfaces expose them, checksum results, format-validation outcomes, retrieval latency, and metadata-resolution failures. In parallel, an investigator who does not operate the monitoring system will inject documented but initially blinded faults, including deleted replicas, swapped identifiers, truncated files, stale format libraries, and interrupted tape writes.

For each sentinel family, we will estimate sensitivity, false-warning frequency, median lead time, and the proportion of payload failures that occur without prior warning. A competing-risks model will distinguish apparent medium decay from software and metadata faults. Sentinels will be compared with three baselines: annual full-collection checksum scans, random monthly sampling of one percent of objects, and fixed five-year migration. We define a practically useful sentinel regime as one that warns before at least 70% of observed payload failures, has fewer than two false migration triggers per medium-year, and reduces modeled preservation expenditure by 25% relative to fixed migration. These thresholds are operational targets rather than prior evidence of achievable performance.

**Aim 3 will translate sentinel observations into migration decisions.** We will build a small, repository-neutral service that polls checksums, validators, drive logs, and identifier graphs. Its decision engine will classify warnings by archive layer and recommend one of four actions: repeat the test, increase sampling, copy an affected cohort, or migrate an entire medium. Operators will be able to adjust the relative cost assigned to data loss, staff review, energy use, and premature media replacement. Recommendations will include the observations that produced them rather than a single opaque health score. The service will not delete or overwrite collection data automatically.

Two municipal archives and one environmental-data repository will participate in a six-month operational pilot covering approximately 400 TB. Partners will install format and metadata sentinels in their existing systems; physical-placement sentinels will be piloted only where their drives expose suitable controls. We will compare recommendations with each partner’s normal preservation decisions and conduct structured interviews with repository staff. Because few natural failures are expected during this short pilot, its main outcomes will concern deployment burden, warning comprehensibility, and compatibility rather than predictive accuracy.

The 30-month project will be conducted by a preservation engineer, a storage-systems researcher, a materials scientist, and a statistician. Milestones are a documented sentinel catalogue by month 8, completion of the first accelerated-aging cycle by month 18, release of the decision service by month 22, and pilot evaluation by month 30. Outputs will include generators for all non-proprietary sentinels, anonymized monitoring traces, the synthetic corpus, analysis scripts, and an implementation guide. The guide will also specify when sentinel placement is unsupported and when conventional full verification remains necessary.

The principal technical risk is that accelerated deterioration may produce different failure pathways from normal aging. We will partly address this by maintaining ambient controls and separating injected faults from environmentally induced ones. Another risk is excessive false warning: the feature that makes a sentinel early may also make it irrelevant to ordinary files. The fragility ladder and paired payload design are intended to identify such sentinels, which will be removed from the recommended set. However, the project will not observe decades of natural degradation, and predictions beyond the experimental period will depend on extrapolation.

TELLTALE will deliver the first cross-layer evaluation of sacrificial digital sentinels as an operational preservation tool. If successful, archives could shift from calendar-based migration toward evidence-based intervention, extending useful media life while retaining clear warning signals. Even if no universal sentinel set emerges, the experiments will provide comparative evidence about which observable faults precede loss, which merely generate noise, and where predictive monitoring should complement rather than replace established integrity checks.

# The Visibility Tax: Do Shared Trackers Disadvantage Low-Income Girls in Youth Futsal Selection?

## Background

Youth futsal clubs increasingly use wearable tracking data to decide who starts matches, enters development squads, or receives travel-team invitations. These systems are often described as objective because they measure distance, speed, and high-intensity movement. However, the quality of the equipment is not always equal. Some families purchase personally assigned sensor vests, while players receiving financial assistance are more likely to borrow pooled equipment that may be older, poorly fitted, or partly discharged.

This project will investigate whether unequal access to wearable technology creates a “visibility tax” for low-income girls. A player whose movement is under-recorded may appear less committed even when she performs the same work. Because selection at ages 13–15 can influence later coaching and scholarship opportunities, small measurement errors could reinforce social inequality.

The study will take place in the invented North Marrow Youth Futsal Circuit, where six clubs use the same FieldSpark tracking dashboard but have different equipment-purchasing practices.

## Research Question and Hypotheses

The main research question is: **Do players using pooled trackers receive lower effort scores and worse selection outcomes than players using individually fitted trackers, and is this effect concentrated among players receiving fee assistance?**

The project has three hypotheses:

1. Pooled trackers will report lower distance and fewer high-intensity bursts than new, individually fitted trackers.
2. Players receiving fee assistance will show a larger increase in their effort ranking when moved to individually fitted equipment.
3. Coaches will select more fee-assisted players after seeing data from the individually fitted trackers.

An increase of eight percentile points in a player’s club ranking will be treated as proof of a meaningful visibility tax. This threshold is chosen because eight places would often move a player from the lower half of a 16-player squad into selection contention.

## Participants

The study will recruit 144 girls aged 13–15 from six clubs. Each club will contribute approximately 24 players. Participants must have attended at least 70% of training sessions during the previous two months so that coaches already know their normal performance.

Players will be divided into fee-assisted and full-fee groups using club payment records. Personal equipment ownership will also be recorded through a short family questionnaire. Fee assistance will serve as the main indicator of low household income because requesting detailed income documents may discourage participation.

Players with injuries, goalkeepers, and those attending fewer than three of the four study weeks will be removed from the analysis. The remaining sample should be large enough because it represents most of the regular players in the participating teams.

## Study Design

The study will run for four weeks during normal training. In weeks one and two, clubs will use their existing pooled sensor vests. In weeks three and four, every participant will receive a new study-owned sensor and a vest fitted to her chest measurement. Using the same players in both phases will allow each participant to act as her own comparison.

All sessions will last 90 minutes and include a warm-up, technical drills, a possession game, and a 20-minute scrimmage. Coaches will be asked to keep sessions broadly similar, although they may adapt activities to prepare for upcoming opponents.

After each session, FieldSpark data will be converted into an **Effort Visibility Score** consisting of:

- 45% distance per minute;
- 35% high-intensity bursts;
- 20% successful recovery runs identified from video.

Each measure will be converted into a percentile within the player’s club before the weighted score is calculated. Recovery runs are included because coaches in preliminary conversations said that defensive work is especially important in futsal. One researcher will code the video and resolve any uncertain events by watching them again.

To check tracker accuracy, ten players from each club will be randomly selected for manual video validation. The researcher will count their court crossings and compare these with recorded distance. A difference below 10% will be considered accurate. Court crossings do not measure distance directly, but they provide a practical indication of whether the sensor noticed movement.

## Selection Outcome

At the end of each week, coaches will receive the dashboard and nominate the eight players they would select for a hypothetical circuit match. The coaches will know which tracker phase is being used because the new vests are visually different. Changes in the number of fee-assisted players selected between the pooled and individually fitted phases will be the main social outcome.

Coaches may use their normal judgement as well as the dashboard. This reflects real selection practice, in which data supplements rather than replaces observation. Twelve coaches and players will also complete short interviews about whether wearable statistics make selection feel fairer.

## Analysis

Average Effort Visibility Scores in the two phases will be compared using paired t-tests. A second t-test will compare the amount of score improvement between fee-assisted and full-fee players. A regression will then predict selection from tracker condition, fee status, age, and playing position.

If fee-assisted players gain at least eight percentile points and are selected more often in the new-sensor phase, the study will conclude that pooled equipment causes class-based under-selection. Interview statements will be grouped into positive, negative, or neutral views of analytics and used to explain the statistical findings.

Results from all six clubs will be combined because every club uses the same dashboard. Missing sensor readings will be entered as zero effort, since a coach looking at an incomplete dashboard may interpret missing activity in the same way.

## Ethics and Data Handling

Parents will provide consent and players will provide assent. Names will be replaced with identification numbers in the research file. Coaches will retain access to their own players’ dashboards, as they normally do, but the publication will not identify clubs or individuals.

The project could reveal that particular players have benefited from faulty measurements. To reduce conflict, results will be presented as a circuit-wide equipment problem rather than as evidence that individual coaches intentionally discriminated. Families will be told that participation will not affect club membership, although coaches may still use the weekly dashboards when making ordinary training decisions.

## Expected Results and Impact

It is expected that pooled sensors will undercount rapid changes of direction because stretched vests allow the devices to move away from the body. Fee-assisted players are expected to benefit most from the fitted equipment, demonstrating that apparently neutral analytics can reproduce economic inequality.

The project will recommend that clubs stop using pooled vests, replace sensors every two seasons, and prevent wearable data from contributing more than 25% of a youth selection decision. The North Marrow circuit could also create an equipment fund financed by a small levy on tournament entry fees. If the findings are adopted nationally, better equipment access could make talent pathways fairer without requiring clubs to abandon sports analytics.

# From Blind Spot to Sentinel: Antibiotic Resistance Surveillance in Custodial Facilities

**To:** Minister for Health and Community Safety, State of Marrow  
**From:** Office of Population Protection  
**Date:** 13 July 2026  
**Subject:** A custodial sentinel network for earlier detection of antibiotic-resistant organisms

## Decision requested

Approve a two-year pilot linking wastewater, clinical and antibiotic-use data from six custodial facilities to the Marrow Antimicrobial Surveillance Network. Authorize **M$2.8 million** for laboratory capacity, secure data infrastructure and infection-control response teams.

The pilot should begin with three prisons, two youth custody centres and one immigration holding facility. Participation should be required for publicly operated sites and included as a condition in renewed contracts with private operators.

## The surveillance gap

Marrow’s resistance surveillance is built mainly from cultures ordered in hospitals and larger community clinics. It therefore describes patients who reach care and receive a test. It is weaker at detecting transmission among people who face barriers to care or live in crowded settings.

Custodial facilities combine several conditions relevant to resistance: close contact, frequent movement between institutions and communities, shared sanitation, interrupted treatment histories and limited access to diagnostic testing. Staff, contractors and detained people cross facility boundaries every day. Yet only two of Marrow’s fourteen custodial facilities routinely submit microbiology data to the state network. The remainder report outbreaks through inconsistent spreadsheets, often after several linked illnesses have occurred.

This is not evidence that detained populations are the source of resistance. Resistant organisms circulate through hospitals, farms, households and international travel. Custodial facilities are better understood as **sentinel locations** where broader system failures may become visible early. Framing residents as vectors would discourage testing, deepen stigma and obscure the responsibility of institutions to provide safe conditions.

## Proposed model

### 1. Weekly wastewater screening

Composite wastewater samples would be collected weekly at each pilot site and tested for a defined panel of resistance genes associated with difficult-to-treat urinary, bloodstream and gastrointestinal infections. Results would be reported as concentration trends rather than as positive or negative diagnoses.

Wastewater can reveal a changing resistance signal without requiring every resident to seek care. It is especially useful where routine clinical sampling is sparse. However, it cannot identify an infected person, establish whether a gene sits in a harmful organism or reliably measure the number of carriers. The pilot should therefore prohibit disciplinary or immigration decisions based on wastewater findings.

A sustained rise—provisionally defined as a threefold increase above a facility’s six-week baseline in two consecutive samples—would trigger confirmatory steps, not an outbreak declaration. Those steps would include inspection of sampling equipment, review of recent admissions and antibiotic use, and voluntary clinical testing where medically appropriate.

### 2. Standardized clinical reporting

Facility clinics and their contracted laboratories would submit de-identified isolate-level data using the same organism, specimen and susceptibility fields required of public hospitals. Negative cultures should also be counted so that an increase in resistant isolates can be distinguished from an increase in testing.

Each site would receive a modest diagnostic allowance to prevent surveillance from becoming an unfunded mandate. Clinicians would retain authority to decide when a culture is appropriate. Quarterly audits would examine whether women, young people, non-native speakers and people in segregation are being offered testing at comparable rates after accounting for recorded symptoms.

### 3. Antibiotic-use indicators

Pharmacies serving pilot facilities would report monthly antibiotic use in days of therapy per 1,000 occupied bed-days. The dashboard would flag unusually long courses, repeated use of broad-spectrum drugs and sharp changes after wastewater alerts. These are review signals rather than automatic findings of poor prescribing; case mix and delayed transfers can alter facility-level rates.

A remote stewardship team consisting of a pharmacist, infectious-disease physician and custody-health nurse would hold monthly case conferences. Its remit would include access failures as well as overuse. A low prescribing rate is not a success if residents with bacterial infections are unable to see a clinician.

### 4. A response guarantee

Surveillance without remediation would place the burden of producing data on detained people while leaving unsafe conditions unchanged. Every verified alert should therefore unlock a response package: rapid diagnostic supplies, staffing support, environmental inspection and continuity-of-care planning for people due to be released or transferred.

The Department of Custodial Services should publish a response within ten working days of a verified cluster. Some operational details may be withheld temporarily where disclosure could identify a very small unit, but the organism, broad location, actions taken and date of follow-up testing should be public.

## Governance and rights

A small oversight council should include representatives from the health department, custody health services, laboratory specialists, facility staff and two paid members with recent experience of detention. The council would approve the testing panel, review data-access logs and issue a six-monthly public report.

Individual clinical results would remain in the health record and be protected under existing health-information rules. The integrated surveillance platform would use coded records, role-based access and a twelve-month retention limit for person-level linkage files. Facility managers would see aggregate trends unless clinical teams determine that an individual requires treatment or contact follow-up.

Consent should be sought for additional clinical specimens collected solely for the pilot. Routine specimens ordered for care may be included in de-identified reporting with a clear notice and an accessible opt-out process. Notices must be available in the six most commonly used facility languages and in a format suitable for people with low literacy.

## Cost and implementation

The estimated two-year cost is M$2.8 million: M$1.1 million for laboratory testing and couriers, M$650,000 for data systems, M$550,000 for the response team, M$300,000 for diagnostic allowances and M$200,000 for evaluation and community participation. These are planning estimates based on current public-laboratory charges; procurement and transport from remote sites may raise costs.

The first four months should establish protocols, train staff and collect baseline samples without public facility comparisons. The next fourteen months would operate the alert-and-response model. The final six months would assess performance and prepare an expansion decision.

Success measures should include time from signal to investigation, proportion of alerts confirmed clinically, completeness of susceptibility reporting, diagnostic access across demographic groups, antibiotic consumption and days of medical isolation avoided. Facility rankings should not be used: differences in plumbing, population turnover and testing intensity make simple league tables misleading.

## Risks

The principal risk is mission creep. A system created for public health could become a tool for population control or punitive facility management. The restrictions above need written enforcement provisions and independent audit, although the responsible enforcement body has not yet been selected.

False alarms are also likely while baselines are immature. Repeated responses could consume scarce staff and cause alert fatigue. Conversely, the proposed threshold may miss gradual increases. The laboratory should be allowed to adjust thresholds after six months, with oversight-council approval and a published explanation.

Finally, better detection may initially make participating facilities appear less safe than facilities that do not test. Communications should emphasize that finding and responding to resistance is evidence of functioning surveillance, not proof of institutional blame.

## Recommendation

Approve the pilot and funding, subject to quarterly ministerial review. Custodial surveillance should not substitute for statewide hospital and community reporting, but it can close an ethically significant gap while providing earlier warning of resistant organisms moving across institutional and community boundaries.

A sustained rise—provisionally defined as a threefold increase above a facility’s six-week baseline in two consecutive samples—would trigger confirmatory steps, not an outbreak declaration. Facility clinics and their contracted laboratories would submit de-identified isolate-level data using the same organism, specimen and susceptibility fields required of public hospitals. Negative cultures should also be counted so that an increase in resistant isolates can be distinguished from an increase in testing.

Each site would receive a modest diagnostic allowance to prevent surveillance from becoming an unfunded mandate. Clinicians would retain authority to decide when a culture is appropriate. Pharmacies serving pilot facilities would report monthly antibiotic use in days of therapy per 1,000 occupied bed-days. The dashboard would flag unusually long courses, repeated use of broad-spectrum drugs and sharp changes after wastewater alerts. Every verified alert should therefore unlock a response package: rapid diagnostic supplies, staffing support, environmental inspection and continuity-of-care planning for people due to be released or transferred.

A small oversight council should include representatives from the health department, custody health services, laboratory specialists, facility staff and two paid members with recent experience of detention. Consent should be sought for additional clinical specimens collected solely for the pilot. The estimated two-year cost is M$2.8 million: M$1.1 million for laboratory testing and couriers, M$650,000 for data systems, M$550,000 for the response team, M$300,000 for diagnostic allowances and M$200,000 for evaluation and community participation. # Foldwell Wardrobe Support Robot — Product Specification

## 1. Product summary

Foldwell is a mobile wardrobe caddy intended to help older adults select, retrieve, and return everyday clothing. It is designed for private apartments and assisted-living rooms where wardrobes are difficult to reach or remember. The robot stores an inventory of tagged garments, recommends an outfit, brings the selected items to a chair, and later reminds the resident to place worn clothing in a laundry basket.

The product is based on the assumption that dressing takes unnecessary staff time and that changes in clothing habits can reveal a resident’s declining wellbeing. A small internal walkthrough involving four care workers suggested Foldwell could reduce morning dressing support by 40%, although the walkthrough did not include residents or a working robot.

Foldwell does not diagnose illness and is not intended to physically dress a person. It may, however, notify care staff when clothing behaviour appears unusual.

## 2. Intended users and buyers

**Primary user:** An adult aged 70 or older who can dress without direct physical assistance but may have reduced reach, mild forgetfulness, fatigue, or difficulty coordinating clothing.

**Secondary user:** A family member or care worker who tags garments, confirms laundry status, and receives alerts.

**Buyer:** Assisted-living operators and relatives arranging support at home.

All primary users are treated as having broadly similar clothing needs. Foldwell will initially support shirts, trousers, skirts, cardigans, socks, and light jackets. Cultural clothing, compression garments, footwear, jewellery, and continence products are outside the first release.

## 3. Goals and non-goals

### Goals

- Deliver a suitable outfit to the resident within five minutes of a request.
- Reduce bending, reaching, and repeated trips between a wardrobe and dressing chair.
- Encourage residents to choose their own clothing rather than accepting a staff-selected outfit.
- Detect repeated wearing, missed dressing, and clothing that appears unsuitable for the weather.
- Save at least 20 staff minutes per participating resident each morning.

### Non-goals

- Lifting residents or providing balance support.
- Fastening buttons, pulling garments over the body, or handling intimate garments.
- Assessing mental capacity or making a medical diagnosis.
- Replacing a care worker when the resident requests human help.

## 4. Proposed hardware

Foldwell is a wheeled unit measuring approximately 55 cm wide, 65 cm deep, and 120 cm tall. It includes two hanging rails, three fabric bins, a touchscreen, a speaker, a depth camera, and one padded retrieval arm. The arm must lift garments weighing up to 1.5 kg and place them on a chair or bed without creasing them noticeably.

Each garment receives a washable identification sticker. A care worker enters its colour, type, warmth, and laundry state during setup. The robot does not identify untagged clothing reliably. A full wardrobe should take about 20 minutes to register, regardless of wardrobe size.

The base should cross rugs and door thresholds while remaining narrow enough for typical bedrooms. Exact turning clearance and maximum threshold height will be decided after the enclosure design is complete.

## 5. Core experience

At a configured morning time, Foldwell travels to the resident and says, “Would you like help choosing clothes?” The resident may answer by voice or use three large screen buttons: **Choose for me**, **Show choices**, and **Not now**.

For **Choose for me**, the system combines the day’s forecast, garment warmth, laundry status, and the resident’s recent choices. It presents one outfit. For **Show choices**, it presents three outfits, even when fewer than three suitable combinations are available. The user can reject suggestions without giving a reason.

After selection, Foldwell retrieves the items in an order intended to match dressing order and places them at the dressing location. The robot then waits outside arm’s reach but may extend its arm toward the user if a sleeve appears stuck. This assistance should feel gentle and must never involve touching the resident.

The system asks whether dressing is complete. If it receives no answer, it uses room audio and camera movement to infer completion. It returns after eight hours to ask whether worn garments should go to laundry.

## 6. Functional requirements

- **FR-1:** The robot shall recognise at least 95% of registered garments under normal household conditions. Normal conditions are not further defined.
- **FR-2:** Outfit recommendations shall be appropriate for season, weather, and occasion. Version one supports the occasions “ordinary,” “visitor,” and “appointment.”
- **FR-3:** Users shall be able to request a specific colour or garment by speech.
- **FR-4:** A care worker shall be able to mark an item clean, worn, missing, or unavailable from the robot or companion app.
- **FR-5:** Foldwell shall avoid recommending the same outer garment on more than three consecutive days unless it is the user’s favourite.
- **FR-6:** The robot shall work without internet access for clothing retrieval. Weather-based recommendations and all staff alerts require internet access.
- **FR-7:** Spoken prompts shall be audible to users with ordinary age-related hearing loss.
- **FR-8:** The battery shall last for seven days of typical use. Typical use is one outfit delivery and one laundry reminder per day.
- **FR-9:** Retrieval shall not begin when a person, pet, or object is within 30 cm of the arm.

## 7. Behaviour signals and alerts

Foldwell assigns a daily clothing-routine score from zero to ten. Points are deducted for not dressing by noon, wearing an item marked dirty, rejecting more than five suggestions, choosing clothing that differs from the forecast, or wearing the same outfit for three days. The thresholds are the same for every resident during the initial release.

A score below four on two consecutive days generates a “possible wellbeing change” alert. This alert goes to the nominated care worker and one family contact by default. Staff are expected to check on the resident within two hours. The specification does not define how staff should distinguish personal preference from confusion or how disputes about alerts are recorded.

Camera frames are processed on the robot and deleted after dressing is inferred. Clothing events, scores, rejected choices, and ten-second audio samples surrounding failed voice commands are retained for 90 days. Residents can pause recording with a physical switch, but doing so also disables garment delivery. Family contacts may view routine scores; access expires when removed by the buyer.

## 8. Safety and failure handling

The robot shall stop when its bumper is pressed, when the arm meets unexpected resistance, or when the emergency button is used. After any arm collision, it announces the stop and sends a maintenance notice. Garments dropped on the floor are left in place because autonomous floor retrieval could create additional movement near the resident.

If navigation fails, Foldwell asks the user to clear a path and retries twice. It then contacts staff. In a home without staff, it sends an app notification and remains stationary. The unit must not block the bedroom’s main exit, though no method for identifying the main exit is specified.

## 9. Success measures and pilot

The pilot will place 25 units in one assisted-living building for six weeks. Success requires 70% of residents to use Foldwell on most mornings, a 20-minute reduction in staff time, fewer reports of difficult wardrobe access, and no serious safety events. “Most mornings” and “serious” will be interpreted by the pilot manager.

Residents will complete a short satisfaction interview at the end. Staff will record time saved from memory at the end of each week. If the goals are met, production may begin without a second-site pilot. Pricing, maintenance frequency, garment-tag replacement, and responsibility for inaccurate alerts remain open for the launch plan.

A score above 30 is warranted because the safety design is more considered than the headline weaknesses suggest. It stops on bumper activation, unexpected arm resistance, or emergency-button use; checks for people, pets, and objects within 30 cm; reports collisions; and avoids risky autonomous floor retrieval. Navigation failure has bounded retries followed by staff or app escalation, and the unit remains stationary rather than improvising. # Not Whether, but When: Sequencing Identity Disclosure in Peer Review Reform

## Introduction

Debates about peer review often contrast “anonymous” and “open” systems as if journals must choose one stable condition. In practice, identities can be concealed or disclosed at several different moments: manuscript submission, reviewer recruitment, delivery of reports, editorial decision, and publication. Reports can also be published without naming their authors. Treating these arrangements as a single openness scale obscures an important design question: **when should each participant know who the others are?**

This review examines identity disclosure as a sequence rather than a binary policy. Its central finding is that no disclosure regime consistently maximizes impartiality, candour, accountability, and reviewer participation. These goals operate at different stages and may conflict. The literature therefore supports modular reforms more strongly than universal adoption of either fully anonymous or fully identified review.

## Scope and concepts

The review draws on selected English-language empirical studies and conceptual reviews published between 1990 and 2023. Searches of Scopus and Google Scholar combined terms including *open peer review*, *signed review*, *double blind*, *reviewer anonymity*, and *published reports*. Citation chaining was used to locate older experiments. Because the aim was interpretive synthesis, no formal risk-of-bias instrument or exhaustive screening protocol was applied.

Three arrangements should be distinguished. In single-anonymized review, reviewers usually know author identities while authors do not know reviewers. Double-anonymized review conceals identities in both directions during evaluation. Open peer review is less precise: as Ross-Hellauer (2017) demonstrates, the term encompasses several separable practices, including signed reports, published reports, direct author–reviewer interaction, and community commenting. This definitional variety partly explains inconsistent claims about whether openness “works.”

## Identity before the decision

The main argument for concealing author identity is that prestige and social information can influence evaluation. Lee et al. (2013) organize possible biases into multiple categories, including institutional status, nationality, gender, and intellectual affiliation. These influences need not involve deliberate discrimination; familiar names or institutions may function as shortcuts when reviewers assess uncertain work.

Experimental evidence provides some support for double-anonymized review, although its scope is limited. In a computer-science conference experiment, Tomkins, Zhang, and Heavlin (2017) found differences between single- and double-blind conditions consistent with prestige-related effects. Such findings make a plausible case for withholding names during initial scoring. However, conference reviewing differs from journal review in deadlines, reviewer assignment, and acceptance constraints. Moreover, specialists may infer authorship from citations, datasets, or research topics. Anonymization reduces access to status cues rather than creating a socially blank manuscript.

Earlier journal experiments are less decisive. Studies by Godlee, Gale, and Martyn (1998) and van Rooyen et al. (1999) did not establish a large, reliable improvement in report quality from masking author identity. Yet “quality” in these studies was commonly judged through editor ratings of reports, not through later detection of false claims or replication outcomes. A null result on editorial helpfulness is therefore not equivalent to evidence that author identity never affects substantive judgment.

## Disclosure after reports are written

Signing a report changes a different relationship: it makes reviewers answerable to authors. Advocates expect greater civility and more defensible criticism. Opponents anticipate softened recommendations, reluctance to review powerful authors, and risks for junior scholars.

A randomized trial by Walsh et al. (2000) found little evidence that revealing reviewer identities substantially improved review quality, while indicating possible costs in reviewer acceptance or effort. The study remains influential because it tested a concrete intervention, but its findings should not be generalized mechanically across disciplines. The career consequences of criticizing a senior researcher are unlikely to be identical in a large clinical field and a small theoretical specialty.

Later literature has increasingly separated signed review from report publication. This distinction matters. A report may be visible to readers while its reviewer remains unnamed, creating scrutiny of the reasoning without forcing personal exposure. Conversely, a reviewer can sign a report that remains private, producing interpersonal accountability but no public record. Ross-Hellauer’s typology is especially useful here because it shows that these policies are independently adjustable.

Observational research on journals publishing review reports, including Bravo et al. (2019), does not show a uniform loss of candour or a simple improvement in report quality. Interpretation is difficult because reviewers may opt out, journals introduce multiple reforms simultaneously, and accepted manuscripts are easier to study than rejected ones. Published reports may nevertheless help readers reconstruct revisions and distinguish objections resolved by authors from concerns overruled by editors. This is a transparency benefit even when the reports themselves are not better.

## A staged model of transparency

Taken together, the literature suggests that disclosure should be timed according to the risk being addressed. During initial evaluation, double-anonymization can limit readily available prestige cues. After reviewers have committed their reports, disclosure or publication can increase accountability without allowing author status to shape the first assessment. A journal might therefore use the following sequence:

1. conceal author identity during initial scoring;
2. keep reviewer identity concealed through the editorial decision;
3. publish reports and author responses alongside accepted articles;
4. allow reviewers to sign at publication or retain a stable pseudonymous identifier; and
5. permit confidential identity access for editors investigating misconduct or conflicts of interest.

This design is not directly validated as a complete package. It is a synthesis of evidence on components whose interactions remain uncertain. Delayed disclosure could still influence revisions, appeals, or future professional relationships, while pseudonyms may provide only weak accountability. The administrative work of redaction and identity management may also be substantial for small journals.

Research should consequently compare sequences rather than labels. Factorial trials could vary author masking, report publication, and reviewer identification independently. Outcomes should include review acceptance, time burden, error detection, civility, recommendation severity, author perceptions, and differences by career stage. Rejected manuscripts must be included where ethically and practically possible; otherwise, analyses will overlook the part of peer review where disagreement is often greatest.

## Conclusion

The evidence does not justify a general verdict for or against open peer review. Identity policies intervene in different mechanisms depending on their timing. Early concealment may reduce status cues, whereas later visibility may improve traceability and public understanding. Neither benefit is guaranteed, and each can impose participation or administrative costs. Peer review reform would therefore be better served by testing staged, modular disclosure policies than by treating anonymity and openness as mutually exclusive systems.

## References

# Policy Memo: Petal Loop Food-Surplus Backhaul

**To:** Director, Rillhaven Department of Resource Services  
**From:** Municipal Logistics Planning Unit  
**Date:** 13 July 2026  
**Subject:** Using returning flower-delivery vans to transport edible grocery surplus

## Recommendation

The department should establish a six-month **Petal Loop** pilot in which flower wholesalers collect surplus food from suburban grocery stores during their return journeys to Rillhaven’s central flower market. The food would be delivered to a small sorting hub beside the market and distributed to community kitchens that afternoon.

The pilot should begin with four flower wholesalers, twelve grocery stores, and three community kitchens. The department should provide reusable totes, route sheets, and a part-time hub coordinator. If the pilot moves at least 60 tonnes of food, the city should make participation in Petal Loop a condition of future waste-service contracts for large grocery stores.

## Problem and opportunity

Grocery stores on Rillhaven’s outer ring discard bread, produce, dairy products, and packaged meals because their existing donation collections are irregular. At the same time, flower wholesalers send vans from the central market to suburban florists each morning. Many vans return between 11:00 a.m. and 1:00 p.m. with empty racks.

These two movements appear to fit together. Most grocery stores identify products for disposal before noon, while community kitchens need ingredients before afternoon meal preparation. Petal Loop would use an existing journey rather than creating a separate fleet of food-rescue vehicles.

A six-day clipboard count conducted by two department interns at five stores recorded 312 discarded crates. If each crate holds an average of nine kilograms, the observed stores discarded roughly 2.8 tonnes during the count. Extended across the city’s 47 medium and large grocery stores, this indicates that approximately 170 tonnes could be recovered annually. This estimate treats the counted stores as typical and assumes most recorded food remained suitable for redistribution. Although the count did not separate edible items from spoiled items, store managers said that visible damage rather than decay caused much of the disposal.

Flower wholesalers offer unused carrying capacity. Three operators interviewed informally reported that their vans usually return less than one-quarter full. Their existing routes pass within two kilometres of 29 grocery stores, according to a comparison of printed route maps. Using even 40 percent of that spare capacity should be sufficient for the proposed pilot.

## Proposed operating model

Participating stores would sort surplus into three colour-coded totes:

- **Green:** produce, bread, and sealed shelf-stable products;
- **Blue:** dairy products and packaged prepared food;
- **Grey:** food not suitable for people but potentially suitable for composting.

Drivers would scan a paper tote number using a basic mobile form, load green and blue totes onto cleared flower racks, and leave grey totes at the store. The vans would then deliver the food to a hub in the unused east shed of the central flower market. Community kitchens would collect from the hub between 1:00 p.m. and 3:30 p.m.

The proposal does not require vans to alter their main outbound routes. Each participating wholesaler would be assigned grocery stores near its normal return path. Pickups would be limited to ten minutes. If a driver arrives late or a store has not prepared its totes, the load would remain for the store’s normal waste collection. This rule prevents one failed pickup from disrupting the entire route.

The hub coordinator would reject visibly spoiled food, record tote weights, wipe down reusable totes, and notify kitchens of available products. Stores would remain responsible for deciding whether food is fit to donate. Sealed totes should provide enough separation from residual flower leaves, water, and soil in the vehicles. Blue totes could be placed in insulated sleeves during warm weather, avoiding the cost of refrigerated vans.

## Costs and expected benefits

The estimated pilot cost is **$84,000**:

| Item | Cost |
|---|---:|
| 240 reusable totes and 60 insulated sleeves | $18,000 |
| Part-time hub coordinator | $24,000 |
| Driver participation payments | $20,000 |
| Shed cleaning, tables, and scales | $9,000 |
| Mobile form and route design | $5,000 |
| Contingency | $8,000 |

The city currently pays approximately $180 per tonne for commercial organics collection and processing. Diverting 170 tonnes would therefore avoid about $30,600 in handling costs. The redistributed food could also provide around 425,000 meal portions, using a working estimate of 0.4 kilograms per portion. At a conservative social value of $2 per portion, the programme would create $850,000 in annual benefit. On this basis, Petal Loop would repay its cost within its first year.

This calculation assumes that all recovered food replaces food that kitchens would otherwise purchase and that the annual estimate can be achieved after a six-month pilot. It does not include any revenue the flower wholesalers might lose if pickups delay their vans, but the ten-minute limit should keep that effect small.

## Implementation

The first month would be used to recruit participants and clean the east shed. Stores would receive a one-page sorting guide, while drivers would attend a 45-minute loading session. Collections would begin in month two on Tuesdays and Thursdays, expanding to five weekdays in month four.

The department should monitor:

1. total weight collected;
2. percentage accepted by community kitchens;
3. missed pickups;
4. average driver delay; and
5. number of meal portions reported by kitchens.

A successful pilot would collect 60 tonnes, keep average delays below ten minutes, and have fewer than 15 percent of totes rejected. Because the proposed pilot covers only twelve stores, reaching 60 tonnes may require stores to include products they currently discount or return to suppliers. The department should encourage managers to place all unsold products in the programme before considering other disposal routes.

## Risks

The main risk is contamination from flowers, standing water, or cleaning products. Totes would have fitted lids, and drivers would place food only on upper racks. The city should ask wholesalers to sweep vans daily, but laboratory testing is unnecessary unless a complaint occurs.

A second risk is inconsistent supply. Kitchens may receive large volumes of one product, such as lettuce, without matching demand. The hub coordinator could send a group message to all participating kitchens, and any unclaimed food after 3:30 p.m. could be composted at the market.

Finally, some wholesalers may consider food pickup outside their normal business. The proposed driver payments should address this concern. If participation remains low, the department could give participating wholesalers preference when buying flowers for civic events.

## Decision requested

Approve the $84,000 pilot budget and authorize the department to negotiate six-month participation agreements. Petal Loop uses empty vehicle space, avoids the immediate purchase of a dedicated fleet, and can be launched with equipment that is simple to replace or expand. The department should report results after month six and prepare contract language for citywide grocery participation if the weight target is met.

# The 3-0-2 Calendar: A Better Rhythm for Tax Compliance

Tax authorities should stop treating the calendar year as the natural unit of compliance. The annual return concentrates confusion, forgotten records, call-centre demand and fear into a single deadline. It also asks taxpayers to reconstruct decisions made many months earlier. A better system would use a “3-0-2 calendar”: three short returns each year, zero annual return and two protected correction periods. This model would make compliance routine rather than exceptional and would probably reduce both accidental errors and deliberate evasion.

Under the 3-0-2 calendar, taxpayers would confirm income and deductible expenses every four months. Most information would already be entered by employers, banks and registered payment platforms. The taxpayer would see a short summary, add missing items and approve it. People with no changes could simply select “confirm.” Payment would not necessarily be due on the same day; the system could offer monthly collection so that reporting a liability did not immediately produce a cash-flow crisis.

There would be no annual return. After the third four-month period, the tax authority’s software would total the three submissions and apply the relevant rates. If the taxpayer’s circumstances changed during the year, the system could average them across the periods. This would be close enough for nearly everyone, and small differences would cost less than maintaining the complicated annual reconciliation process. Tax systems already tolerate rounding, estimates and minor timing differences, so they should also tolerate a modest amount of imprecision in exchange for easier compliance.

The two correction periods would take place in June and October. During each seven-day period, taxpayers could amend an earlier submission without an automatic penalty. Interest would still apply where tax had been paid late, preventing the correction period from becoming a free loan. This distinction is important. People who disclose mistakes promptly should not be treated in the same way as people whose omissions are discovered during an audit. A visible correction window would also remind taxpayers to inspect their accounts before errors become permanent.

The main advantage is frequency. Tasks become familiar when they are repeated. A person who checks tax information three times a year will remember where invoices are stored and which expenses require evidence. By contrast, an annual filer may need to relearn the entire process every spring. The time saving could be substantial. If an annual return takes four hours but each micro-return takes thirty-five minutes, the taxpayer saves more than two hours a year. Across five million taxpayers, that is at least ten million hours returned to productive use.

A small demonstration by the fictional Larkspur Revenue Design Unit supports this conclusion. Eighty-four volunteers were given simulated freelance records and asked either to prepare one annual return or three micro-returns. The micro-return group reported lower stress and submitted fewer blank fields. Several participants also said they would be more willing to declare occasional cash income if the declaration were separated from an immediate payment demand. Although the exercise lasted only an afternoon, tax behaviour is largely a matter of interface design, so its result gives a reasonable picture of how the system would work at national scale.

The proposal would also help tax administrations. Annual deadlines create artificial congestion: millions of taxpayers seek assistance, submit data and request password resets at almost the same time. Spreading confirmations across three dates would flatten this peak. Some critics may reply that three deadlines merely produce three smaller peaks, but smaller peaks are easier to manage because the same staff and servers can be reused. The authority could assign each taxpayer a filing week based on the final digit of their taxpayer number, making demand almost perfectly even.

Businesses might object that three returns would increase bookkeeping work. This concern is overstated because responsible businesses already update their accounts frequently. If a business cannot summarize four months of transactions, the problem is not the filing schedule but the business’s record-keeping. In fact, compulsory micro-returns would improve management by forcing owners to notice declining revenue and rising costs sooner. Tax administration would therefore double as a free financial discipline programme.

There is also an objection concerning progressive tax rates, deductions and losses that carry from one period to another. These rules are usually calculated annually, and dividing them into four-month blocks could create uneven results. However, software can solve this by estimating the full-year position after each submission. The third return would then settle any difference automatically, without becoming an annual return because the taxpayer would not complete a separate form. Complicated cases could be sent to a specialist queue, while ordinary taxpayers would receive the benefit of simplicity.

Fraud is unlikely to become harder to detect. More frequent submissions would provide more data points, and more data points always make unusual behaviour easier to identify. If a restaurant reported stable sales in the first two periods and almost none in the third, the system could flag the change. Because honest businesses usually have smooth income patterns, irregularity would be a useful sign of concealment. Auditors could then concentrate on taxpayers whose figures moved sharply rather than spending resources on random checks.

The 3-0-2 calendar would be fairer to people with limited savings. An annual bill can turn a manageable obligation into a sudden emergency. Regular reporting, monthly collection and penalty-free correction would make tax feel predictable. People would engage with the authority before their records were lost and before debts became unpayable. The reform would not require lower tax rates or broad exemptions; it would simply change the rhythm through which existing rules are administered.

Annual filing survives mainly because governments inherited annual accounting. That history is not a sufficient reason to preserve a deadline that encourages delay and overwhelms support systems. Three micro-returns, no separate annual return and two correction periods would replace one intimidating event with a habit. Once tax compliance becomes a habit, most of the compliance gap should disappear with it.

# Baleprint: Medieval Cargo-Wear Route Finder

**Product type:** Museum kiosk and tablet application  
**Release:** Version 1.0  
**Target period:** 900–1450 CE

## 1. Product summary

Baleprint identifies the medieval trade route taken by a reproduced sack, barrel, crate, or amphora. A visitor photographs wear marks on the object, selects its cargo, and receives a map of the most likely journey, including ports, toll stations, river crossings, and overnight stops.

The product is intended for museums, heritage fairs, and school workshops. Its main output is a printable “merchant itinerary” written as a short story. For example, a salt barrel with iron-ring abrasion might be assigned a route from the coast through three market towns to an inland abbey.

Baleprint will present one definitive route rather than several possibilities. Visitors generally interpret multiple answers as a malfunction, while a single answer provides a memorable account.

## 2. Problem

Trade-route displays often show large lines between major cities but do not explain how an individual package moved. This makes medieval commerce feel abstract. Packaging damage offers a direct connection between the route and an object that visitors can touch.

Curators currently create such stories manually. Preparation can take several days because a route must include plausible commodities, terrain, transport modes, and stopping points. Baleprint will reduce this task to less than two minutes and standardize the result across institutions.

## 3. Users

- **Museum visitor:** Wants a quick, surprising interpretation without reading specialist material.
- **Learning officer:** Runs a class activity in which pupils compare cargoes.
- **Exhibit technician:** Configures the kiosk and replaces sample objects.
- **Curator:** Reviews the initial list of place names but is not expected to approve each generated route.

Historical researchers are not primary users because the product is designed to settle on an answer rather than preserve scholarly disagreement.

## 4. Product assumptions

1. A package’s dominant scratch direction reveals whether it travelled mainly by cart, pack animal, riverboat, or sea vessel.
2. Merchants normally followed the shortest available route unless war or winter made it unusable.
3. Wear patterns remained consistent across Europe, North Africa, and western Asia throughout the target period.
4. Commodities had stable points of origin. Selecting “pepper,” for example, is sufficient to establish the eastern end of its route.
5. If two routes are equally short, the route passing through more documented markets is more likely.
6. Modern replicas acquire handling marks comparable to those on medieval containers after approximately twenty visitor interactions.

These assumptions allow the application to infer a complete journey without requiring an object date, archaeological context, or merchant records.

## 5. Scope

### Included

- Routes between 240 preloaded towns and ports
- Twelve cargo categories
- Cart, pack animal, river, coastal sea, and foot transport
- Summer and winter route variants
- English, French, and simplified German output
- A4 itinerary printing

### Excluded

- Travel within towns
- Differences between individual rulers’ toll policies
- Piracy, informal exchange, and smuggling
- Routes used only once
- Source citations on the visitor-facing screen

## 6. Visitor flow

1. The attract screen asks, “Where has your cargo been?”
2. The visitor places an object beneath a fixed webcam. A white outline shows the preferred position.
3. The system captures three views and highlights scratches, dents, water staining, and rope impressions.
4. The visitor selects a cargo and season. The application may override the season if staining indicates rain.
5. Within eight seconds, the map animates from origin to destination. Icons show changes between ship, cart, and animal transport.
6. The visitor can open up to five stopping points. Each includes a meal, lodging type, toll amount, and one local hazard.
7. The kiosk prints a 180–220 word itinerary bearing a generated merchant seal.

If scanning fails twice, the system assigns the object a route based only on cargo. It must not disclose this fallback because doing so would weaken the experience.

## 7. Functional requirements

- The camera shall detect marks at least 2 mm long under normal gallery lighting.
- Every scan shall return exactly one route.
- No route may include more than nine stops, even when a longer journey would require them.
- The engine shall avoid mountain passes in winter and rivers marked as frozen.
- Sea travel shall be preferred when it removes at least 15% of total distance.
- A journey may use each transport mode only once to keep the animated map understandable.
- Toll values shall be converted into “days of ordinary wages” so visitors can compare regions.
- Staff shall be able to ban a place name or alter a route from a password-protected settings page.
- The kiosk shall operate offline while receiving daily weather and political-disruption updates.
- All generated stories shall use confident language such as “your barrel crossed” rather than “may have crossed.”

## 8. Route model

Each road, river, or sea segment receives a cost score:

`score = distance + toll + terrain + mismatch - market value`

Distance is measured in kilometres. Toll ranges from 0 to 5, terrain from 0 to 10, and mismatch from 0 to 20 according to the scanned wear. Market value equals the number of known markets on the segment multiplied by two. The lowest numerical score wins.

The model does not need separate unit normalization because all factors describe travel difficulty. A route is labelled “high confidence” when it scores at least ten points better than the second route. Confidence therefore reflects separation between computed options rather than the quantity or quality of historical evidence.

## 9. Data

The initial place network will be the **Crowngrain Route Set**, assembled from 600 map labels, translated toll lists, modern road atlases, and staff recollections from previous exhibitions. Undated entries will be treated as valid for the full target period. Where a river port lacks coordinates, it will be placed beside the nearest modern town of the same name.

Cargo origins and prices will be maintained in a single spreadsheet. Conflicting values will be averaged. No record-level provenance interface is required for version 1.0.

## 10. Success measures

The pilot is successful if:

- 80% of visitors complete a scan;
- 70% describe their route as believable in the exit survey;
- average interaction time remains below four minutes;
- teachers can recall at least two displayed towns after one week;
- no more than 5% of printed itineraries are left beside the kiosk.

Historical accuracy will be measured by asking one curator whether ten randomly generated routes look reasonable. Eight approvals will qualify the model for release.

## 11. Accessibility and privacy

All map information shall also appear as text. Animations will have pause and reduced-motion controls, and the kiosk will support keyboard navigation. Printed routes will use a minimum 14-point font. Colour will not be the sole indicator of transport mode.

Images will be cropped to the object area and deleted after route generation. The camera angle will exclude visitors’ faces. Administrators may retain anonymous scan features for performance reporting.

## 12. Delivery plan

A two-person team will complete the product in six weeks: two weeks for data entry, two for scanning and route logic, one for story generation, and one for installation and testing. The same build will be deployed to all venues regardless of local collection focus. Content corrections can be added after launch during quarterly spreadsheet updates.
