# The Archive Is the Rehearsal: Designing Digital Storage Around Recovery

Long-term digital storage is often described as a problem of finding durable media. This encourages questions such as whether tape lasts longer than hard drives, whether archival optical discs are worth their price, or whether a cloud provider can preserve an object for a century. Those questions matter, but they begin too late in the story. A storage medium can retain every bit entrusted to it while the information still becomes unusable.

A more useful starting point is the recovery event. Imagine that the original staff have left, the normal software is unavailable, and one copy has already failed. Can a new custodian locate the right material, verify it, interpret it, and produce a usable result without guessing? Long-term storage is the maintenance of that complete recovery path.

This perspective changes what counts as preservation work. Copying files is necessary, but so are documenting units, retaining transformation code, testing credentials, recording rights, and periodically asking someone to restore material under constrained conditions. The archive is not merely the collection of stored objects. It is also the organization’s repeatedly demonstrated ability to recover them.

## A marsh archive that outlived its instruments

Consider the fictional Merewick Tidal Office, which has monitored an estuary since 1978. Its collection includes handwritten observations transcribed into spreadsheets, voltage readings from obsolete conductivity probes, photographs of gauge installations, calibration certificates, database exports, and recent high-frequency sensor streams. Researchers want to use the record to study long-term changes in salinity.

The office’s oldest digital files are still readable. That is not enough. A column marked `S2` contains values between 0 and 4,095, but no surviving file says whether these are salinity measurements or raw readings from a 12-bit converter. A later dataset records timestamps without a time zone. One period was adjusted using a calibration curve stored in an employee’s personal analysis folder. Several photographs show instruments, but their filenames do not identify which station they depict.

Nothing in this example requires dramatic bit decay. The files can remain perfectly intact while the evidence they once carried slowly separates from its context. Conversely, an archive can survive the loss of a particular disk if it has redundant copies, trustworthy manifests, and enough documentation to reconstruct meaning.

Merewick therefore treats every important dataset as a recoverable package rather than as a loose set of files. The package includes data, descriptions, checksums, provenance, and, where needed, executable transformations. The office also performs recovery exercises in which a staff member who did not create the package must use it.

## Four layers of survival

A practical preservation plan has to protect at least four layers.

### 1. Bits

The bytes must remain available and unchanged. Media failure, accidental deletion, malicious alteration, interrupted transfers, and silent corruption all threaten this layer. Replication and fixity checking primarily protect bits.

### 2. Objects

The bytes must still form identifiable files, database records, disk images, or other bounded objects. A raw stream copied from a damaged disk may preserve bytes without preserving the original directory structure. A database export may omit attachments stored in another directory. Object-level preservation asks what belongs together and whether the set is complete.

### 3. Meaning

A future user must know what the objects represent. Units, coordinate systems, time zones, missing-value codes, character encodings, calibration histories, and relationships between tables can be more important than the choice of medium. Meaning also includes distinctions such as whether a file is an original observation, a corrected derivative, or a presentation copy.

### 4. Authority

The user must be able to judge where the material came from and whether it is an acceptable version. Provenance, chain of custody, signatures, access restrictions, and records of later transformations belong here. Two files can contain identical-looking tables while having very different evidential value.

These layers are related but not interchangeable. A checksum can establish with high confidence that an object matches a prior bit sequence, but it cannot establish that the column labels are accurate. A detailed catalogue cannot compensate for the loss of every data copy. A successful opening of a file does not prove that it is the approved version.

## Begin with a threat model, not a shopping list

Storage systems fail in different ways, and extra copies help only when they do not share the same failure. Three replicas in one synchronized account may all receive the same mistaken deletion. Two tape sets stored in one room may be lost in the same flood. A cloud copy and an office server may both depend on credentials held by one departing administrator.

A modest archive should consider at least these threats:

- physical media failure;
- silent changes to stored data;
- accidental deletion or overwriting;
- ransomware or misuse of privileged accounts;
- fire, water, heat, theft, and building access failures;
- loss of encryption keys or account credentials;
- unsupported hardware interfaces and software formats;
- incomplete transfers and undocumented processing;
- supplier closure, contract disputes, and unaffordable retrieval fees;
- disappearance of the people who understand the collection.

The aim is not to predict one disaster. It is to avoid arrangements in which one event can disable every recovery route. This is why independence matters more than the raw number of copies. Independence can mean different buildings, administrative accounts, media types, operating systems, or responsible staff. Not every copy needs every kind of independence, but the collection should not have a single invisible hinge.

Threat modelling also prevents exaggerated attention to bit rot. Random media decay is real, yet routine human actions often create faster losses. A well-meaning employee can empty a synchronized folder in seconds. An export script can silently omit records for years. A preservation plan that buys premium media but does not test exports is badly balanced.

## Inventory before preservation

An institution cannot preserve material it cannot enumerate. An initial inventory should record more than filenames and sizes. For each collection, it should identify an owner, a responsible custodian, the approximate volume, file types, sensitivity, retention requirement, dependencies, current locations, and the consequences of loss.

The inventory does not have to describe every item at first. Merewick begins at collection level: gauge photographs, raw probe output, laboratory assays, calibration records, and published annual summaries. It then adds item-level descriptions where distinctions affect recovery.

This process often reveals that the apparent archive is a mixture of sources and outputs. A rendered chart may be reproducible from raw data and code, but only if the code and parameters survive. A database backup may look comprehensive while excluding files stored outside the database. Temporary working data may contain unique annotations despite having an unimportant name.

Priorities should follow value rather than volume. Merewick assigns material to three broad classes:

1. **Irreplaceable evidence:** original observations, calibration records, and signed reports.
2. **Costly but reproducible material:** cleaned datasets and derived products whose source and transformation survive.
3. **Convenience copies:** caches, duplicated downloads, and outputs that can be generated automatically.

The distinction determines replication and testing effort. It also gives staff permission to delete material that adds cost without adding evidence. However, value can change, and seemingly minor files sometimes explain major datasets. Classification therefore needs periodic review rather than a single disposal campaign.

## Build bounded preservation packages

Loose files are difficult to move and verify because nobody knows where the collection ends. A preservation package gives the material a boundary. A simple package might contain:

- a stable package identifier;
- the preserved data objects;
- a machine-readable file manifest;
- checksums for every object;
- a short human-readable description;
- provenance and acquisition notes;
- format, encoding, unit, and time-zone information;
- known omissions and defects;
- rights or access conditions;
- transformation code and parameters, if derivatives matter;
- a record of preservation actions.

The manifest should use relative paths so that the package can move without rewriting every reference. It should also avoid making the checksum file validate itself, which creates a circular definition. A second, separately stored catalogue can record the expected checksum of the package manifest.

Packages should be large enough to preserve meaningful relationships but small enough to transfer and inspect. Merewick uses a working ceiling of 50 gigabytes for most packages, dividing larger sensor collections by station and year. This is an administrative rule rather than a technical boundary, but it makes failed transfers less expensive to repeat and gives recovery exercises manageable units.

Compression can reduce storage and transfer costs, but a single huge compressed archive increases the blast radius of corruption and can make partial retrieval difficult. For collections with millions of tiny files, packaging may still be worthwhile because filesystems and object stores handle small-object overhead poorly. The correct choice depends on access patterns: frequently retrieved items benefit from individual addressing, while deep archival sets may benefit from grouped containers.

## Fixity: knowing whether the bits moved

A cryptographic checksum is a compact value calculated from an object’s bytes. If an object changes, recalculating the checksum will almost always produce a different value. SHA-256 is a sensible default for preservation manifests because it is widely implemented and accidental collisions are for practical purposes negligible.

Checksums are most useful when created near acquisition, verified after every transfer, and checked periodically afterward. Generating a checksum only after a damaged file has spent ten years in storage merely records the damaged state. The checksum manifest must itself be protected and versioned; otherwise an attacker or faulty process could replace both a file and its expected checksum.

A mismatch proves that two observed bit sequences differ, but it does not by itself identify the correct one or explain the cause. The archive needs a known-good copy, provenance records, or an earlier trusted manifest to repair the damage. Matching checksums establish continuity of bits, not truth of content.

Merewick verifies all newly written packages immediately. It checks its online holdings quarterly and samples offline holdings annually. This creates a regular signal without requiring every tape or disc to be mounted each quarter. The office treats a failed check as an incident: it preserves the suspect version, compares replicas, records the repair, and verifies the replacement.

## Copies must fail differently

The familiar advice to keep three copies on two kinds of storage with one copy off-site is a useful memory aid. It is not a complete design. Media diversity is less important than failure diversity. Two brands of hard drive connected to the same compromised server are not meaningfully independent.

Merewick’s irreplaceable class has three principal copies:

- an online copy in the office storage system for access and routine verification;
- a cloud object copy in a separate administrative account with version retention and deletion delays;
- an offline tape copy stored at a regional records depot.

The catalogue and checksum manifests also exist outside the main storage account. At least two people can retrieve credentials through a documented escrow procedure. The cloud account does not use the same identity provider as the office network, reducing the chance that one account compromise disables both.

Offline storage is valuable because it interrupts automatic propagation. A tape in a depot cannot immediately receive a ransomware encryption operation or synchronized deletion. Yet offline copies create their own risks: they are harder to inspect, slower to retrieve, and easily forgotten. An offline copy with an unreadable label or an unavailable drive is more comforting than useful.

Geographic separation should reflect plausible regional events. Moving a copy to another room protects against a disk failure but not against a building fire. Moving it across town may not protect against a flood affecting the whole estuary. Greater distance, however, raises transport, legal, and coordination costs. Independence is therefore an engineering trade-off, not a ritual.

## What the media can and cannot do

No storage medium is archival by itself. Its useful lifetime depends on manufacturing quality, environmental conditions, write quality, handling, interfaces, and the institution’s ability to inspect and migrate it.

### Hard-disk systems

Hard drives offer fast access and low initial cost. In an actively managed array, failed devices can be detected and replaced without waiting for a scheduled archive visit. This makes disk suitable for frequently used material and routine fixity checks.

A powered array is nevertheless an operating service, not a shelf object. Controllers, firmware, power supplies, filesystems, and administrator actions are part of its risk surface. Redundant array layouts can maintain availability after a drive failure, but they are not backup: deletion and corruption can be replicated across the array.

### Data tape

Tape offers high capacity and low power consumption while stored. It can provide a strong offline layer and is economical for collections retrieved infrequently. Its disadvantages are operational. Drives are expensive, cartridges must be tracked, and generations of tape technology eventually lose convenient support. Restoring one small object may require locating and mounting a whole cartridge.

Tape is best treated as a continuing programme. Merewick assumes that cartridges will be copied to a supported generation about every seven years. Actual timing should respond to drive availability and error reports rather than to the calendar alone, but a scheduled cycle prevents indefinite postponement.

### Optical media

Recordable optical discs can be useful for small, closed collections. Finalized write-once media resist ordinary remote overwriting and offer straightforward physical separation. Capacity is limited, large sets become labour-intensive, and quality varies among discs and writers. Claims of extremely long laboratory life do not guarantee that a future office will possess a compatible drive.

Optical media are therefore a niche layer rather than Merewick’s primary store. The office uses them for a small set of annual legal deposit packages, with duplicate discs and periodic test reads.

### Solid-state storage

Flash drives and consumer solid-state drives are convenient transfer devices but weak unattended shelf archives. Charge retention, controller failure, and uncertain behaviour after long periods without power make their future readability difficult to predict. Enterprise solid-state systems can be reliable when monitored, but that is different from placing a portable drive in a drawer for fifteen years.

### Cloud object storage

Cloud services can provide geographic replication, integrity features, versioning, access logs, and rapid scaling. They transfer some hardware operations to a specialist provider. They do not transfer preservation responsibility. The customer must still maintain accounts, pay bills, configure retention correctly, preserve metadata, and test exports.

Cloud failure may take the form of a policy change or an inaccessible account rather than a broken disk. Retrieval charges can make a technically recoverable collection financially awkward to leave. A useful cloud plan includes an exit procedure, an estimate of full-export time, and a copy of the object inventory held elsewhere.

## Preserve the read path, not every old machine

A file’s read path is the chain needed to turn stored bytes into intelligible content. It may include a container format, codec, application, runtime, operating system, license service, hardware architecture, credentials, and external reference files. Recording this chain exposes dependencies that a file extension conceals.

There are two main responses to format obsolescence. Migration converts material into a currently supported format. Emulation recreates enough of the old environment to run original software. Migration improves ordinary access but can alter features. Emulation can preserve behaviour but requires its own technical knowledge and may depend on old licenses or undocumented hardware.

For common tabular data, Merewick retains the original file and creates a normalized export with documented character encoding, explicit missing values, and unambiguous dates. For a specialized instrument database, it preserves the original backup, a set of open table exports, the database schema, screenshots of important views, and a virtual-machine image containing the reader software.

The virtual machine is not assumed to be permanent. It is another object that must be stored and tested. A future hypervisor may not open it directly, and network-dependent licensing may fail. The open exports provide a simpler fallback even if they do not reproduce every feature.

Merewick reviews formats every five years and migrates any format that has lost ordinary support. This interval creates a predictable responsibility, although some formats may remain safe for decades while a proprietary service can become inaccessible within months. Significant supplier changes should trigger an earlier review.

## Recovery exercises reveal hidden dependencies

Routine checksum verification answers whether selected bytes still match. A recovery exercise asks whether the archive can actually deliver useful information. The distinction resembles checking that emergency equipment is present versus conducting an evacuation drill.

A useful exercise begins with a request rather than a storage device. For example: recover all raw and corrected observations from Station Alder for March 1996, identify the calibration applied, and produce a table of salinity values with timestamps in coordinated universal time. The operator receives the catalogue and documented credentials but no help from the original data creator.

The exercise should record:

- time required to locate and retrieve the package;
- whether every expected object was present;
- results of checksum verification;
- hardware, software, and accounts used;
- ambiguities encountered in documentation;
- whether a usable output could be produced;
- corrective actions, owners, and deadlines.

Merewick restores at least one percent of its preservation packages each year, weighted toward high-value and technically unusual holdings. New formats are included early, and older untested packages receive priority. The office also performs a complete catalogue-and-credential exercise after major staffing or supplier changes.

Sampling cannot prove that every package is recoverable. It can, however, expose systemic defects such as expired accounts, missing tape drives, malformed manifests, or instructions that make sense only to their author. The sample should rotate and should not be selected solely from easy packages. A superficially high success rate is meaningless if difficult holdings are always excluded.

An external or newly appointed participant is especially valuable. Experienced custodians unconsciously supply missing context. If a package works only because one person remembers that negative values mean a sensor was out of water, the documentation has failed even though that person can complete the task.

## A failed drill can be a preservation success

In one Merewick exercise, a technician retrieves a 2004 conductivity package from tape. Its checksums match, the comma-separated tables open, and the calibration document is present. The final salinity calculation still cannot be reproduced because the package refers to `curve_final.dat`, which is absent.

An employee eventually finds the file in an old project directory. Investigation shows that the original packaging script included only files with three approved extensions. The missing calibration table used an unrecognized extension and had been excluded from forty-two packages.

The office repairs the affected packages, changes the script to work from explicit dependency lists, and adds a completeness report to future ingest. The tape did not fail. The package definition did. Only a task-oriented recovery exercise revealed the problem.

This illustrates why drills should not be judged solely as pass-or-fail performances. Their purpose is to discover dependencies while repair is still possible. An archive that reports no recovery problems may be exceptionally well run, or it may be asking questions too narrow to reveal them.

## Storage economics includes human attention

Media prices are easy to compare because they have visible units. Staff time, retrieval delays, audit work, and dependency maintenance are harder to price but often dominate a long-lived archive. A very cheap offline copy can become expensive if every request requires manual cartridge handling. A convenient cloud service can become expensive when a full migration incurs large retrieval charges.

A basic cost estimate should include acquisition, replication, monitoring, catalogue work, environmental control, replacement hardware, migrations, test restores, and eventual exit from each supplier. It should also include growth. Keeping three copies of a collection that doubles every two years is a different commitment from preserving a closed historical deposit.

Merewick reduces cost by applying service levels. Irreplaceable evidence receives three independently managed copies and annual sampled recovery. Reproducible derivatives receive two copies and can be regenerated when practical. Convenience material may have only short retention. This arrangement is less simple than declaring every byte equally permanent, but it concentrates effort where loss would matter most.

The classification has limits. Regeneration costs can rise, source software can disappear, and future research value is difficult to foresee. For that reason, the office records disposal decisions and keeps small contextual files even when it discards bulky intermediate outputs.

## A compact operating cycle

Merewick’s preservation work follows a repeating cycle:

1. **Acquire:** transfer material into a staging area without altering the source copy.
2. **Inspect:** identify formats, scan for obvious hazards, and compare the transfer with the source.
3. **Describe:** record provenance, meaning, rights, dependencies, and known defects.
4. **Package:** create bounded objects, manifests, and checksums.
5. **Replicate:** write copies into distinct failure domains and verify each write.
6. **Monitor:** check fixity, account status, capacity, media errors, and supplier changes.
7. **Exercise:** restore selected packages and answer realistic questions with them.

# The Revision Budget Protocol: Testing Whether Scarcity Labels Improve Peer Review

## Abstract

Peer review often produces long lists of requests without indicating which requests matter most. Editors may ask authors to “address all comments,” even when reviewers disagree or when some comments would require an entirely new project. This proposal tests a simple reform called the **Revision Budget Protocol**. Under the protocol, each reviewer receives ten priority credits to allocate across requested revisions. A major request costs three credits, a minor request costs one credit, and a non-mandatory observation costs no credits. Reviewers cannot submit more priced requests than their budget permits. Authors see the credit value attached to each request, and editors are encouraged to use those values when preparing decision letters.

The protocol will be introduced at six journals in the Meridian Scholarly Cooperative and compared with standard review at six other journals. Approximately 1,800 manuscripts are expected during a nine-month enrolment period. Primary outcomes will be time from first decision to resubmission, number of revision requests, and editor-rated manuscript improvement. Secondary outcomes will include reviewer agreement, author satisfaction, acceptance time, six-month citation counts, and post-publication corrections. Quantitative analysis will compare mean outcomes between protocol and standard-review manuscripts. Interviews with authors, reviewers, and editors will explore whether the budget makes expectations clearer.

The central prediction is that visible scarcity will prompt reviewers to distinguish necessary criticism from optional preference. This should reduce review inflation, make revision letters easier to interpret, and shorten publication delays without lowering article quality. If successful, the protocol could be added to common manuscript systems with little continuing cost.

## 1. Background and rationale

Peer review is usually treated as a problem of obtaining enough expert judgment. Less attention is given to the allocation of that judgment. A reviewer can request a new robustness analysis, a rewritten introduction, three additional experiments, different terminology, and a new theoretical framework without having to rank those requests. The resulting report may be thoughtful in every detail but unmanageable as a whole. Editors can resolve this problem, yet many decision letters simply reproduce reviewer reports and instruct authors to respond point by point.

This creates what this proposal calls **revision inflation**: the tendency for review rounds to accumulate requests because no participant bears a visible cost for adding one more request. The cost is instead paid by authors through additional work and by journals through delay. Revision inflation does not require reviewers to be careless. A reviewer may reasonably mention every weakness that occurs to them, since the current interface does not distinguish a decisive objection from an attractive improvement. When two or three reviewers follow the same logic, the combined request can exceed what any one reviewer would consider proportionate.

Existing reforms commonly focus on reviewer identity, report publication, checklists, reviewer training, or changes in compensation. Those approaches may improve accountability, but they do not directly limit the volume of requested work. Checklists can even add requirements. Training is difficult to maintain, while paying reviewers may increase the supply of reports without improving their prioritization. The Revision Budget Protocol instead changes the structure of the task at the moment comments are entered.

The idea is adapted from constrained planning. When decision-makers must distribute a fixed quantity of points, they reveal priorities that remain hidden in an unrestricted list. A ten-credit limit should make a reviewer consider whether a fourth major demand is more important than the first three. It also gives the editor a common unit for comparing reports. For example, if two reviewers each allocate three credits to concerns about the identification strategy, while a third assigns one credit to figure colours, the editor has an immediate signal about where the revision should concentrate.

An informal test was conducted by the Cooperative’s Methods and Workflow Group using 48 previously completed reviews in the internally assembled **Bramble Review Set**. Three graduate assistants retrospectively assigned credits to the requests. Reports containing more than ten apparent credits had taken authors an average of 41 days longer to answer than reports below the limit. This result supports the expected relationship between review volume and delay, although the retrospective coders did not always agree on where one request ended and another began. The proposed study moves from retrospective coding to prospective use by actual reviewers.

The reform does not prevent criticism. Reviewers may include unlimited zero-credit observations, which are displayed to authors under the heading “Suggestions and Context.” Priced comments appear under “Required Priorities.” The distinction is intended to preserve intellectual discussion while preventing every suggestion from becoming a condition of publication.

## 2. Conceptual model

The proposal treats author attention as a scarce resource. Every requested revision draws on that resource, but standard review makes its scarcity invisible. A fixed review budget is expected to operate through three mechanisms.

First, it should create **reviewer triage**. Reviewers will reserve credits for defects that affect the reliability or intelligibility of the manuscript. Preferences about style, additional citations, or extensions will tend to move into the zero-credit category.

Second, it should create **editorial comparability**. Editors currently receive reports written in different tones and formats. Credit allocation provides a numerical summary that can be combined across reviewers. A concern receiving six total credits appears more important than one receiving a single credit.

Third, it should create **author certainty**. Authors frequently devote substantial effort to guessing which comments are essential. A visible allocation tells them where work is most likely to affect the final decision. Greater certainty should lead to faster revision and fewer defensive response letters.

These mechanisms imply that fewer mandatory requests will improve both speed and quality. Concentrating effort on highly priced concerns should produce larger improvements than distributing effort across an unrestricted set of comments. The protocol may therefore avoid the usual trade-off between faster publication and rigorous evaluation.

Credits represent both the importance of a concern and the amount of author effort it justifies. These concepts are closely related because important concerns normally deserve more work. Reviewers will not be asked to estimate hours, since such estimates would vary by author expertise and available data. Instead, the major-versus-minor distinction will serve as a sufficiently consistent approximation.

## 3. Research questions and hypotheses

The study will address five questions:

1. Does a fixed reviewer budget reduce the time required to revise a manuscript?
2. Does it reduce the number and length of mandatory requests?
3. Do manuscripts improve as much under budgeted review as under standard review?
4. Do authors and reviewers perceive the process as clearer and fairer?
5. Does numerical prioritization increase agreement among reviewers?

The following hypotheses will be tested:

- **H1:** Protocol manuscripts will be resubmitted at least 20% faster than standard-review manuscripts.
- **H2:** Protocol reports will contain fewer mandatory requests and fewer total words.
- **H3:** Accepted protocol manuscripts will receive improvement ratings no more than 0.25 points below accepted control manuscripts on a five-point scale.
- **H4:** Authors and reviewers in the protocol group will report higher satisfaction.
- **H5:** Reviewers assigned to the same manuscript will show greater convergence in their judgments, measured by the proportion of credits allocated to the same topic category.

## 4. Intervention

The intervention will be built into **Ravel**, the Cooperative’s manuscript management system. Reviewers will encounter the ordinary free-text report box followed by a “Revision Priorities” panel. They will convert each requested author action into one of three entries:

- **Major priority: three credits.** A problem that could affect the manuscript’s central claim, method, or interpretation.
- **Minor priority: one credit.** A bounded change that improves accuracy or presentation but does not alter the central claim.
- **Suggestion or context: zero credits.** An optional idea, extension, reading recommendation, or stylistic preference.

Each reviewer receives ten credits. Unused credits disappear when the report is submitted and cannot be transferred to another reviewer. Reviewers may revise their allocation until submission. The system prevents submission when priced entries exceed ten credits, but it does not limit the length of an entry or the number of zero-credit observations.

Topics are selected by reviewers from a menu. The dashboard does not automatically sum requests that use different wording, so the editor decides whether two entries refer to the same concern.

An editor may grant up to five **emergency credits** when reviewers identify a serious matter but have exhausted their budgets. Emergency credits must be accompanied by a one-sentence explanation. There is no formal limit on zero-credit suggestions because optional scholarly exchange is considered beneficial.

Authors will receive a colour-neutral table listing required priorities first and suggestions second. They will be asked to respond to all priced requests. They may decline zero-credit suggestions without a detailed defence. A short statement will explain that credit values indicate editorial priority rather than a direct estimate of labour.

## 5. Study design and participants

The Meridian Scholarly Cooperative publishes twelve journals covering experimental ecology, computational linguistics, ceramic engineering, regional economics, archival studies, educational measurement, and related areas. All twelve have agreed to participate. Six will use the Revision Budget Protocol, while six will continue standard review.

Migration order is set by the Cooperative’s technical office and can therefore be treated as random for research purposes. In practice, the first group includes journals whose managing editors have completed data-cleaning work and confirmed that they are ready to migrate. No journal will switch condition during the study.

The enrolment period will last nine months. Based on the previous year, the journals are expected to receive about 1,800 submissions that enter external review. Roughly 1,050 should receive at least one revise-and-resubmit decision. Reviewers working for more than one participating journal may encounter both systems, which will permit experience with the budget to spread into control reviews. This is unlikely to be substantial because most Cooperative reviewers complete only one report per year.

Authors will not choose a study condition because condition is determined by journal. They will be informed of the journal’s review format when the first decision is issued. The primary operational outcome will be **revision duration**, defined as calendar days from the first revise-and-resubmit decision to receipt of the revised manuscript. The second primary outcome will be the number of mandatory requests in the first-round reports. For standard reviews, two research assistants will divide report text into requests and classify each as major, minor, or optional. Disagreements will be resolved by the project manager. The protocol group will use the entries created by reviewers.

The primary quality outcome will be **editor-rated improvement**. At acceptance, handling editors will compare the original and final manuscript and answer four questions about methodological reliability, clarity, evidential support, and contribution. Each item will use a five-point scale, and the mean will form an improvement score. Editors necessarily know which review system they used, but their direct familiarity with the manuscripts makes them the most efficient judges.

Secondary measures will include:

- days from submission to final decision;
- number of review rounds;
- word count of reviewer reports and author response letters;
- proportion of requests completed by authors;
- author, reviewer, and editor satisfaction on five-point scales;
- reviewer invitation acceptance rates;
- six-month citations for published articles;
- corrections or retractions recorded within six months of publication; and
- topical convergence between reviewers.

Surveys will be sent immediately after each participant completes their role. To reduce burden, they will contain six rating questions and one optional comment box. A purposive group of 20 authors, 20 reviewers, and 12 editors will also be interviewed. Selection will seek a mixture of positive and negative survey ratings. Interviews will ask how participants interpreted credits, whether they changed their allocation of effort, and whether important issues were omitted.

The project team will download system logs monthly. Manuscript titles will be replaced with numerical identifiers in the analysis file. Journal names will remain visible because disciplinary differences are relevant to interpretation.

## 7. Analysis plan

Mean revision duration in the two conditions will be compared with an independent-samples t-test. Request counts, report word counts, satisfaction scores, improvement scores, and citations will be tested in the same way so that results are readily comparable. Outcomes with strongly uneven distributions will first be log-transformed. A two-sided significance threshold of 0.05 will be used.

The analysis will treat manuscripts as independent observations. Although manuscripts are grouped within journals, each manuscript receives a separate set of authors and usually separate reviewers, so dependence should be limited. Journal discipline will be added as a control variable in a supplementary regression if the protocol and control means differ at baseline. Manuscripts with missing survey data will be omitted from the relevant satisfaction analysis.

H3 will be supported if the mean editor-rated improvement in the protocol group is no more than 0.25 points below the control mean. H5 will be supported if protocol reviewers allocate a larger share of their comments to matching topic categories than the categories assigned by research assistants to control reports.

Interview transcripts will be divided among three team members, who will identify repeated themes. Themes mentioned by at least five participants will be described in the final report. Representative quotations will illustrate common experiences. The qualitative findings will explain unexpected numerical results but will not change whether the hypotheses are accepted.

A successful result will require support for H1 and H3, plus improvement in at least one of H2, H4, or H5. If revision is faster but editor ratings decline by more than the margin, the protocol will be considered unsuitable for full implementation. Corrections and retractions will be monitored as a safety indicator, although the expected number is small.

## 8. Feasibility, governance, and ethics

The Cooperative already controls the Ravel codebase, and its product team estimates that the priority panel and editor dashboard can be completed in eight weeks. The intervention does not require additional reviewers, author payments, or changes to journal scope. Reviewers will receive a two-minute explanation when opening the form. Editors will have access to a one-page guide during the study.

The project will be overseen by a steering group consisting of the principal investigator, two managing editors, one software engineer, and one author representative. The group will meet every two months. Editors may report urgent failures, such as an inability to submit a review, directly to the software engineer.

The protocol is considered a modification of editorial workflow rather than human-subject experimentation, so individual consent will not be requested for use of routine timing and report data. Survey and interview participation will be voluntary, with a consent checkbox. Reports will be quoted only after removing names and manuscript-specific details. Data will be stored on the Cooperative’s server for five years.

A possible concern is that reviewers may omit a crucial issue after spending their credits. Emergency credits and unlimited suggestions provide safeguards. Editors also retain authority to reject a manuscript or request additional work regardless of the displayed budget.

## 9. Timeline and resources

Months 1–2 will be used for interface development, assistant training, and preparation of survey instruments. The six-week pilot will begin in month 3, followed by full enrolment from months 4 through 12. Follow-up of revisions and accepted manuscripts will continue through month 16. Analysis and reporting will occur in months 17 and 18.

The requested budget is 164,000 Meridian dollars. It includes 62,000 for a half-time project manager, 38,000 for two part-time research assistants, 24,000 for software development, 12,000 for interview transcription, 8,000 for participant gift vouchers, and 20,000 for investigator and administrative costs. Authors will not be compensated for routine participation. Interview participants will receive a 40-dollar voucher.

The main deliverables will be an implementation manual, anonymized outcome tables, reusable Ravel interface modules, and a report to the Cooperative’s editorial council. If the success criteria are met, the protocol will be activated at the six control journals at the beginning of the following publication year.

## 10. Expected contribution

Peer review reform often asks participants to become more diligent, transparent, or generous. The Revision Budget Protocol instead changes the choice architecture of the report. It makes priority visible and asks reviewers to spend a finite resource when imposing work on authors. This is a modest technical change, but it could address the widespread accumulation of requests more directly than additional guidance.

The study will provide evidence on whether constrained commenting shortens revisions and whether numerical priorities can function across disciplines. It will also produce practical information about how reviewers use zero-credit suggestions, how editors interpret aggregated credits, and whether authors direct more effort toward central concerns. A favourable result would justify broad adoption of revision budgets as a low-cost route to faster, more focused peer review.

For standard reviews, two research assistants will divide report text into requests and classify each as major, minor, or optional. Disagreements will be resolved by the project manager. The protocol group will use the entries created by reviewers.

The primary quality outcome will be **editor-rated improvement**. At acceptance, handling editors will compare the original and final manuscript and answer four questions about methodological reliability, clarity, evidential support, and contribution. Each item will use a five-point scale, and the mean will form an improvement score. Editors necessarily know which review system they used, but their direct familiarity with the manuscripts makes them the most efficient judges.

Secondary measures will include:

- days from submission to final decision;
- number of review rounds;
- word count of reviewer reports and author response letters;
- proportion of requests completed by authors;
- author, reviewer, and editor satisfaction on five-point scales;
- reviewer invitation acceptance rates;
- six-month citations for published articles;
- corrections or retractions recorded within six months of publication; and
- topical convergence between reviewers.

Surveys will be sent immediately after each participant completes their role. To reduce burden, they will contain six rating questions and one optional comment box. A purposive group of 20 authors, 20 reviewers, and 12 editors will also be interviewed. Selection will seek a mixture of positive and negative survey ratings. Interviews will ask how participants interpreted credits, whether they changed their allocation of effort, and whether important issues were omitted.

The project team will download system logs monthly. Manuscript titles will be replaced with numerical identifiers in the analysis file. Journal names will remain visible because disciplinary differences are relevant to interpretation.

## 7. Analysis plan

Mean revision duration in the two conditions will be compared with an independent-samples t-test. Request counts, report word counts, satisfaction scores, improvement scores, and citations will be tested in the same way so that results are readily comparable. Outcomes with strongly uneven distributions will first be log-transformed. A two-sided significance threshold of 0.05 will be used.

The analysis will treat manuscripts as independent observations. Although manuscripts are grouped within journals, each manuscript receives a separate set of authors and usually separate reviewers, so dependence should be limited. Journal discipline will be added as a control variable in a supplementary regression if the protocol and control means differ at baseline. Manuscripts with missing survey data will be omitted from the relevant satisfaction analysis.

H3 will be supported if the mean editor-rated improvement in the protocol group is no more than 0.25 points below the control mean. H5 will be supported if protocol reviewers allocate a larger share of their comments to matching topic categories than the categories assigned by research assistants to control reports.

Interview transcripts will be divided among three team members, who will identify repeated themes. Themes mentioned by at least five participants will be described in the final report. Representative quotations will illustrate common experiences. The qualitative findings will explain unexpected numerical results but will not change whether the hypotheses are accepted.

A successful result will require support for H1 and H3, plus improvement in at least one of H2, H4, or H5. If revision is faster but editor ratings decline by more than the margin, the protocol will be considered unsuitable for full implementation. Corrections and retractions will be monitored as a safety indicator, although the expected number is small.

## 8. Feasibility, governance, and ethics

The Cooperative already controls the Ravel codebase, and its product team estimates that the priority panel and editor dashboard can be completed in eight weeks. The intervention does not require additional reviewers, author payments, or changes to journal scope. Reviewers will receive a two-minute explanation when opening the form. Editors will have access to a one-page guide during the study.

The project will be overseen by a steering group consisting of the principal investigator, two managing editors, one software engineer, and one author representative. The group will meet every two months. Editors may report urgent failures, such as an inability to submit a review, directly to the software engineer.

The protocol is considered a modification of editorial workflow rather than human-subject experimentation, so individual consent will not be requested for use of routine timing and report data. Survey and interview participation will be voluntary, with a consent checkbox. Reports will be quoted only after removing names and manuscript-specific details. Data will be stored on the Cooperative’s server for five years.

A possible concern is that reviewers may omit a crucial issue after spending their credits. Emergency credits and unlimited suggestions provide safeguards. Editors also retain authority to reject a manuscript or request additional work regardless of the displayed budget.

## 9. Timeline and resources

Months 1–2 will be used for interface development, assistant training, and preparation of survey instruments. The six-week pilot will begin in month 3, followed by full enrolment from months 4 through 12. Follow-up of revisions and accepted manuscripts will continue through month 16. Analysis and reporting will occur in months 17 and 18.

The requested budget is 164,000 Meridian dollars. It includes 62,000 for a half-time project manager, 38,000 for two part-time research assistants, 24,000 for software development, 12,000 for interview transcription, 8,000 for participant gift vouchers, and 20,000 for investigator and administrative costs. Authors will not be compensated for routine participation. Interview participants will receive a 40-dollar voucher.

The main deliverables will be an implementation manual, anonymized outcome tables, reusable Ravel interface modules, and a report to the Cooperative’s editorial council. If the success criteria are met, the protocol will be activated at the six control journals at the beginning of the following publication year.

## 10. Expected contribution

Peer review reform often asks participants to become more diligent, transparent, or generous. The Revision Budget Protocol instead changes the choice architecture of the report. It makes priority visible and asks reviewers to spend a finite resource when imposing work on authors. This is a modest technical change, but it could address the widespread accumulation of requests more directly than additional guidance.

The study will provide evidence on whether constrained commenting shortens revisions and whether numerical priorities can function across disciplines. It will also produce practical information about how reviewers use zero-credit suggestions, how editors interpret aggregated credits, and whether authors direct more effort toward central concerns. A favourable result would justify broad adoption of revision budgets as a low-cost route to faster, more focused peer review.

# Trellis A425 Product Specification

**Product:** Trellis A425 Acoustic Farm Monitor  
**Release:** Pilot 1.0  
**Status:** Build approval candidate  
**Owner:** Pelagos Loom Systems  
**Primary deployment:** Suspended kelp and shellfish farms in coastal ocean water

## 1. Product summary

Trellis A425 is a two-channel passive acoustic monitoring node for offshore farms. It has two related purposes:

1. Detect acoustic patterns associated with loose fittings, repeated line impacts, sudden tension releases, and nearby vessel activity.
2. Produce a calibrated record of the surrounding soundscape without treating every sound generated by farm infrastructure as biological activity.

Farm operators currently inspect submerged hardware on a schedule or after visible damage. Ecologists working at the same sites may deploy separate recorders, but farm-generated clicks, rattles, and cable strum can contaminate those recordings. A425 combines these workflows. It labels likely infrastructure noise at the edge, sends low-bandwidth event summaries to shore, and retains calibrated audio for later review.

The product consists of an underwater listening node, an optional surface gateway, retrieval software, and the HarborDesk web application. The node can operate for a complete service interval without the gateway. When a gateway is present, alarms and health summaries are relayed to shore; continuous raw audio remains on the node.

A425 is intended to prioritize inspections and improve interpretation of farm soundscapes. It is not a structural safety instrument, a species detector, or a substitute for physical inspection.

## 2. Problem and opportunity

Long-line farms contain shackles, droppers, floats, bridles, tensioners, and crop-bearing lines that move differently as biomass and weather change. Some defects become repetitive acoustic sources before they are visible at the surface. A loose connector may strike on every wave cycle, while a damaged line may emit a short broadband transient when fibers or attachments fail.

The same sounds can distort ecological monitoring. A recorder may count thousands of farm-hardware impulses during rough weather, producing an apparent increase in acoustic activity unrelated to animals. Operators and researchers therefore need a shared record that preserves the audio while distinguishing likely hardware, vessel, weather, and biological contributions.

The initial commercial opportunity is farms of 20 to 200 hectares that already make monthly or quarterly maintenance visits. One A425 node is expected to cover a representative farm section rather than every component. Dense installations may use one node per 250 metres of backbone line.

## 3. Goals and non-goals

### 3.1 Goals

- Notify an operator of persistent hardware-like chatter within 15 minutes when a gateway is available.
- Capture short, high-resolution audio around sudden tension-release events.
- Retain a continuous, calibrated low-band recording for at least one nominal 90-day deployment.
- Separate likely farm noise from broad biological and environmental sound categories with confidence values.
- Give technicians enough diagnostic information to decide whether an inspection should be brought forward.
- Export audio, event labels, calibration history, and device-health data in documented formats.
- Remain useful during gateway, backhaul, or positioning outages.

### 3.2 Non-goals

- Certifying that moorings, lines, or farm structures are safe.
- Pinpointing a sound to a particular shackle or crop line.
- Identifying animal species or estimating abundance.
- Recording human speech intentionally.
- Providing collision avoidance or navigation warnings.
- Streaming continuous audio to shore.
- Operating as an active sonar. The node's acoustic modem transmits only short data bursts outside configured quiet periods.

## 4. Users and key decisions

### 4.1 Farm operations lead

The operations lead monitors several sites and decides whether to schedule a vessel visit. This user needs concise alarms, a trend view, and an indication of uncertainty. They do not need to inspect spectrograms for routine events.

### 4.2 Field technician

The technician installs, retrieves, cleans, and tests nodes. They need a mobile workflow that functions without shore connectivity, records mounting details, and verifies both hydrophone channels before leaving the site.

### 4.3 Acoustic analyst

The analyst reviews clips, corrects classifications, exports calibrated data, and compares farm and reference periods. They need access to provenance, model version, clipping status, and unmodified waveform samples.

### 4.4 Research coordinator

The coordinator defines quiet periods, retention rules, and data exports for a study. A research coordinator may view operational events but cannot acknowledge maintenance alarms unless also assigned the operator role.

## 5. Operating assumptions

A425 is designed around the following initial deployment envelope:

| Parameter | Supported range |
|---|---:|
| Water depth | 12–60 m |
| Listening-node depth | 5–45 m |
| Water temperature | -2–30 °C |
| Current speed | Up to 2.2 m/s sustained |
| Service interval | 30–90 days |
| Surface-gateway distance | Up to 700 m slant range |
| Farm section represented by one node | Up to 250 m radius |
| Typical vessel access | Monthly or less frequent |

The node may be mounted on a weighted independent line or on a farm backbone through the supplied elastomeric isolator. Independent mounting is preferred for ecological studies. Backbone mounting is faster but transmits more structure-borne vibration into the enclosure.

Coverage radius is an operational planning value, not a guarantee that every fault within 250 metres will be audible. Bathymetry, bottom type, farm density, sea state, and mounting strongly affect propagation.

## 6. System architecture

### 6.1 Underwater listening node

The node contains:

- Two factory-calibrated hydrophones on a rigid 0.8 m vertical spar.
- Independent low-noise preamplifiers and 24-bit analogue-to-digital channels.
- A low-power processor for detection, feature extraction, compression, and health monitoring.
- A 2 TB removable solid-state storage cartridge.
- A 2.1 kWh rechargeable battery pack.
- Pressure, temperature, tilt, and enclosure-humidity sensors.
- A low-rate acoustic modem for event and health messages.
- A mechanical release eye and a high-visibility recovery pennant.

The two hydrophones provide redundancy and coherence information. They are not a sufficient array for reliable source localization.

### 6.2 Surface gateway

The optional Spar A4 gateway is attached to a farm float or a dedicated marker. It receives event summaries from up to eight nodes and forwards them through the available shore backhaul. It stores seven days of summaries if backhaul is unavailable.

The gateway does not request retransmission while a node is recording a configured quiet period. Emergency health messages, including leak detection, override this rule.

### 6.3 HarborDesk

HarborDesk stores fleet state, alerts, annotations, and selected clips. It presents data through a browser interface and a versioned export interface. A desktop retrieval tool imports raw cartridges directly when internet service is unavailable.

## 7. Functional requirements

Priority terms are **Must**, **Should**, and **Could**. A Must requirement blocks the pilot release if unmet.

### 7.1 Acoustic acquisition

| ID | Priority | Requirement |
|---|---|---|
| ACQ-01 | Must | Record two synchronized channels at 24 kHz and 24-bit depth during baseline operation. |
| ACQ-02 | Must | Switch both channels to 96 kHz for an event window of at least 20 seconds before and 40 seconds after a trigger. |
| ACQ-03 | Must | Maintain a circular high-rate buffer so pre-trigger audio is preserved. |
| ACQ-04 | Must | Keep inter-channel sample skew below 10 microseconds. |
| ACQ-05 | Must | Store factory sensitivity by serial number and apply it only as metadata; original integer samples shall remain available. |
| ACQ-06 | Must | Mark samples affected by clipping, dropped blocks, modem transmission, or clock correction. |
| ACQ-07 | Should | Support scheduled recordings at 48 kHz for research protocols. |
| ACQ-08 | Should | Suspend high-rate event capture when remaining storage is below 5%, while retaining baseline audio and event summaries. |

The target hydrophone sensitivity is -165 dB re 1 V/µPa, with unit-specific calibration supplied from 20 Hz to 40 kHz. The useful baseline band is 40 Hz to 11 kHz. High-rate event clips use a 40 Hz to 42 kHz band. Levels displayed in HarborDesk are referenced to 1 µPa.

### 7.2 Time and calibration

| ID | Priority | Requirement |
|---|---|---|
| CAL-01 | Must | Timestamp audio in coordinated system time with less than 100 ms accumulated error over 90 days after a valid pre-deployment synchronization. |
| CAL-02 | Must | Store clock-offset estimates before deployment and after retrieval. |
| CAL-03 | Must | Play an internal electrical reference signal through each acquisition channel at startup and once every 24 hours. |
| CAL-04 | Must | Flag a channel when reference amplitude changes by more than 1.5 dB from its deployment baseline. |
| CAL-05 | Should | Permit an analyst to attach a post-deployment piston-calibrator result to the deployment record. |

The electrical reference verifies electronics but does not test the hydrophone ceramic or its exposure to water. The field application therefore requires a tap and ambient-noise comparison between channels during installation.

### 7.3 Edge detection and classification

The node shall detect six top-level event classes:

- **Persistent hardware chatter:** repeated impulses or tonal knocks with timing consistent with moving farm components.
- **Tension-release transient:** an isolated high-energy broadband event with a rapid onset.
- **Vessel near-field:** sustained engine, propeller, or cavitation-like energy passing through the monitored band.
- **Weather dominated:** elevated flow, rain, wave, or mooring noise that reduces interpretability.
- **Biophony pulse:** non-vessel, non-hardware acoustic activity with temporal or spectral structure learned from reviewed examples.
- **Unknown:** an event exceeding capture criteria without a sufficiently confident class.

Each event record shall include class probabilities, start and end times, peak calibrated level, one-third-octave summaries, channel coherence, clipping state, and model version.

| ID | Priority | Requirement |
|---|---|---|
| DET-01 | Must | Detect a persistent chatter candidate after at least 30 qualifying impulses in 10 minutes. |
| DET-02 | Must | Close a chatter event after 20 minutes without a qualifying impulse. |
| DET-03 | Must | Capture tension-release candidates whose 100 ms broadband level exceeds the rolling median by 18 dB on either channel. |
| DET-04 | Must | Reduce chatter confidence when similar impulses occur during modem transmission or when tilt varies by more than 8 degrees. |
| DET-05 | Must | Preserve events below the alert threshold for later analysis. |
| DET-06 | Should | Allow site-specific alert thresholds without replacing the underlying class probabilities. |
| DET-07 | Could | Learn the dominant repetition period of an acknowledged hardware source and group subsequent occurrences. |

During the first 48 hours of a deployment, alerts are held in calibration state while the node calculates ambient percentiles. Leak, storage, and battery alarms are not held. After calibration, the default chatter alert requires a class probability of 0.78 and persistence across three consecutive analysis windows.

### 7.4 Alerts

HarborDesk shall support four alert types:

1. **Inspection suggested:** persistent hardware chatter or repeated tension-release events.
2. **Acoustic coverage degraded:** weather dominance, channel failure, clipping, or excessive flow noise.
3. **Device attention:** low battery, low storage, clock fault, abnormal tilt, or gateway loss.
4. **Leak/retrieve:** enclosure humidity or pressure behaviour consistent with water ingress.

Alerts must display the triggering evidence, confidence, node state, and recommended next action. Recommended actions shall use cautious language such as “review recent clips and inspect the monitored section when practicable.” They shall not state that a line is safe or has failed.

In connected operation, 95% of inspection-suggested summaries shall reach HarborDesk within 15 minutes of the event being closed. In disconnected operation, the alert shall appear after the next successful relay or cartridge import with its original event time intact.

Operators can acknowledge, defer, or close an alert. Closure requires a reason: inspected/no defect, inspected/defect found, known source, weather artefact, test event, or other. These outcomes are retained as model-evaluation labels.

## 8. Soundscape outputs

For each local hour, A425 produces:

- Equivalent broadband sound level for the baseline band.
- 5th, 50th, and 95th level percentiles.
- Proportion of valid recording time dominated by vessel, weather, hardware, biophony, and unknown classes.
- Number of impulsive events by class.
- A data-quality score based on channel health, clipping, flow noise, and missing samples.
- A “farm-adjusted acoustic activity” series that excludes windows classified as hardware or vessel dominated.

Farm-adjusted acoustic activity is a filtering aid, not a biodiversity index. HarborDesk shall keep the unadjusted series beside it and show hours removed from the calculation. Analysts can change class exclusions, but exported results must record those choices.

The standard comparison view displays a selected farm node against either its own historical baseline or a user-designated reference node. It does not automatically claim that differences were caused by farming activity.

## 9. User experience

### 9.1 Fleet page

The fleet page shows each node as normal, calibration, degraded, attention, or retrieve. Status is based on the most severe active condition. The page displays the age of the last message so that a normal state is not confused with a silent gateway.

### 9.2 Event review

An event page includes a playable clip when uploaded, waveform, spectrogram, event features, both channel levels, and nearby tilt and weather-dominance estimates. Analysts can relabel an event and explain the correction. The original machine label remains immutable.

Because only selected clips reach shore, the interface shall distinguish “no clip uploaded” from “audio missing.” A request for a non-uploaded clip is placed in the retrieval manifest for the next cartridge import; it cannot be fulfilled remotely from a disconnected underwater node.

### 9.3 Field application

The field application guides a technician through node scan, clock synchronization, storage check, battery check, mounting photographs, depth entry, channel tap test, acoustic-modem test, and deployment activation. All steps except modem test are mandatory. A supervisor can waive a failed modem test because the recorder remains functional without it.

## 10. Data and exports

Audio is stored in one-hour lossless files with a companion manifest. Event clips are separate references into the original recording rather than destructive copies. If high-rate event audio exists, it is linked to the baseline interval.

Every deployment receives a unique identifier and records node serial number, hydrophone serial numbers, firmware, model version, calibration table, mounting type, nominal position, depth, and operator-entered notes.

Exports shall include:

- Lossless waveform files with calibration sidecars.
- Hourly metrics in comma-separated tables.
- Event and annotation records in structured text.
- A deployment manifest with checksums.
- An audit record of threshold and label changes.

HarborDesk retains event metadata for five years by default and uploaded clips for 180 days. Administrators can set clip retention from 7 to 365 days. Raw cartridges are managed by the customer and are not automatically erased after import.

## 11. Security and access

Each node and gateway has a unique manufacturing identity and accepts signed firmware packages. Gateway-to-shore messages are encrypted and rejected if replayed outside the permitted sequence window. Device credentials are replaced during depot service or after a suspected compromise.

HarborDesk uses role-based access for administrators, operators, technicians, analysts, and read-only guests. Changes to alert thresholds, retention settings, and event labels are logged with user and time.

Audio near working vessels may incidentally contain machinery patterns or indistinct voices transferred through hulls. Access to raw clips is therefore limited to analysts and administrators by default. The product does not attempt automatic speech recognition or speaker identification.

A lost node protects its configuration and event index with storage encryption. Continuous waveform files are encrypted on the cartridge but become readable through the desktop retrieval tool when the deployment key is available.

## 12. Reliability and serviceability

The enclosure shall withstand 100 m equivalent static pressure without permanent deformation and pass a 72-hour pressure soak at 75 m equivalent depth. External parts shall tolerate fouling removal with plastic scrapers and low-pressure freshwater. Copper-based exposed antifouling surfaces are not permitted on the hydrophone faces.

The battery and storage cartridge are depot-replaceable, not user-replaceable on a small vessel. A technician shall be able to exchange the complete node in under 15 minutes without removing the farm mounting collar.

The endurance target is 90 days under the reference profile: baseline recording continuously, six high-rate events per day, one acoustic summary exchange every 15 minutes, and water temperature of 12 °C. The node shall reserve enough energy to transmit a daily low-battery message for seven days after baseline recording stops.

When one hydrophone channel fails, baseline recording continues on the remaining channel and all classifications are marked degraded. When storage writes fail, the node retries on a reserved partition, stops high-rate capture, and transmits a device-attention alarm. A leak indication shuts down charging and nonessential electronics but preserves one final health transmission if power remains.

## 13. Verification and pilot acceptance

### 13.1 Bench verification

- Inject calibrated tones and transients into both channels across the supported band.
- Verify sample skew, gain error, clipping flags, file checksums, and clock drift.
- Run a 100-day accelerated storage simulation using generated audio.
- Cycle the node through 200 pressure changes between surface pressure and 60 m equivalent depth.
- Confirm signed-update rejection, replay rejection, role boundaries, and encrypted-cartridge recovery.
- Measure endurance using the reference event profile in a 20 °C tank room.

### 13.2 Controlled-water verification

A suspended test rig shall include a loose steel connector, polymer line impacts, a controlled fiber break, a small workboat pass, and playback of reviewed biological and weather recordings. Tests will be conducted at three ranges between 10 and 150 metres. The event log from synchronized cameras and load sensors will serve as ground truth.

The pilot model passes controlled-water evaluation when it achieves:

- At least 85% recall for persistent hardware chatter episodes.
- No more than two false inspection alerts per node-week.
- At least 80% recall for controlled tension-release transients above the specified trigger contrast.
- At least 90% correct separation of vessel-dominated and hardware-dominated test windows.

### 13.3 Farm pilot

Twelve nodes will be deployed across three farms at Morrow Shoal, Bellweather Reach, and Orison Inlet. Each site will include one independently mounted node and farm-mounted nodes. The pilot will span one high-growth period and one post-harvest period, with at least 120 node-days of valid audio overall.

Operators will inspect the monitored section after every high-confidence inspection alert where weather permits. They will also inspect a random sample of non-alert weeks to estimate missed persistent faults. Acoustic analysts will review 300 randomly sampled event windows and all tension-release alerts without seeing the machine label first.

Pilot acceptance requires:

- Ten of twelve nodes completing their planned deployment without water ingress.
- Median connected alert latency below 15 minutes.
- Fewer than three false inspection alerts per node-month after the 48-hour calibration period.
- At least 75% agreement between analysts on the six top-level classes.
- At least 80% of operators rating the alert evidence sufficient to make an inspection decision.
- No loss of a complete hour file after a recoverable power interruption.

Performance shall be reported separately for independent and farm-backbone mounting. Results from inaccessible alerts will be categorized as unverified rather than assumed false.

## 14. Deployment and support plan

Pilot customers receive one planning session, installation templates, a spare node for every six deployed units, and remote review of the first 48-hour calibration report. Pelagos Loom Systems performs battery and seal service annually or after six deployments, whichever occurs first.

Release proceeds in three gates:

1. **Engineering gate:** bench, pressure, security, and file-integrity tests complete.
2. **Limited-water gate:** controlled-water detection targets met and no unresolved leak mechanism.
3. **Farm gate:** twelve-node pilot acceptance complete, with installation guidance updated from mounting comparisons.

The first commercial release supports one geographic language, one shore time zone per fleet, and up to 200 nodes per HarborDesk account. Multi-fleet aggregation and automated work-order integration are deferred.

## 15. Principal risks and mitigations

| Risk | Consequence | Planned mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Structure-borne farm noise overwhelms waterborne sound | Excess alerts and biased soundscape metrics | Isolating mount, dual-channel coherence features, separate reporting by mounting type |
| Heavy fouling changes hydrophone response | Drift in calibrated levels | Smooth guards, pre/post calibration, 30-day channel comparison trend |
| Unknown farm designs differ from training data | Reduced classification accuracy | Preserve unknown class, site calibration, analyst corrections, model versioning |
| Acoustic modem creates detectable noise | Contaminated recordings | Mark transmission windows and prohibit scheduled traffic during quiet periods |
| Gateway loss is mistaken for node failure | Unnecessary retrieval | Display message age separately; preserve local recording |
| High-rate triggers exhaust storage | Loss of event detail late in deployment | Daily trigger budget, event grouping, low-storage mode |
| Operators interpret absence of alerts as proof of safety | Missed physical defect | Persistent interface disclaimer and continued scheduled inspection guidance |
| Animal calls resemble repetitive hardware sounds | Misclassification | Retain audio, show confidence, require persistence and cross-feature checks |

## 16. Open product decisions

Before commercial release, the team must decide whether customers can upload their own classifier packages, whether cartridges remain customer-owned or are exchanged through a service pool, and whether reference nodes require a lower-cost configuration without a gateway modem. These decisions do not block the twelve-node pilot but affect service pricing, support responsibility, and data comparability.
